maison.etymology: Inherited from Old French maison ('dwelling, house'), from Classical Latin mansionem (nominative mansio, 'a staying, remaining, night quarters, inn'), derived from manere, mansum ('to remain, dwell, stay the night'), which displaced domus in Gallo-Romance.

majeur.etymology: Borrowed/adapted from Classical Latin majorem (nominative major, 'greater, larger, elder', comparative of magnus 'great', learned doublet of maire); as a noun (le majeur), denotes the middle (longest) finger.

history.meaning: greater, larger, of full legal age
greater, major, of legal age (adj.); middle finger (noun)

mal.etymology: Inherited from Old French mal ('evil, harm, pain, illness; badly'), from Classical Latin malum ('evil, misfortune, harm', neuter of adjective malus 'bad, evil') and adverb male ('badly, ill').

malheureusement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from the feminine adjective malheureuse ('unfortunate, unhappy', from malheur 'bad luck, misfortune' < Old French mal + eür < Latin malum augurium 'ill omen') + adverbial suffix -ment.

malin.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (feminine maligne) from Classical Latin malignus ('of an evil or grudging nature, spiteful, stingy', from malus 'bad' + -gnus < gignere 'born'); in popular French, le Malin ('the Evil One, the Devil, renowned for his cunning') softened the word's everyday sense to 'clever, shrewd, mischievous'.

history.meaning: malignant (in medicine); shrewd, clever, sly (in everyday speech)

maman.etymology: Affectionate nursery word formed by reduplication of the syllable ma- (attested in French since the 13th c., parallel to Latin mamma and Greek mamme), with nasalization of the final vowel in French.

manche.etymology: Feminine la manche ('sleeve') is inherited from Classical Latin manica ('long tunic sleeve reaching over the hand, handcuff'), derived from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: shirt or coat sleeve; narrow sea channel (la Manche)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: manche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: manche

manche.notes: Masculine **le manche** ('broom or pan handle') comes from a closely related Latin derivative *manicus* ('part held in the hand').

manger.etymology: Inherited from Old French mangier ('to eat'), from Late/Vulgar Latin manducare ('to chew, chomp, eat ravenously', derived from Manducus, a comic mask with chomping jaws, from Classical Latin mandere 'to chew'), which displaced Classical edere in Gallo-Romance and Italian.

manquant.etymology: Present participle of manquer ('to be lacking, be missing'), used as an adjective and noun since the 16th–17th century.

manquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian mancare ('to be lacking, fail, fall short'), derived from Classical Latin mancus ('maimed in the hand, crippled, defective, incomplete', source of Old French manc / manchot).

history.meaning: to be defective, fall short, be lacking
to miss, lack, run short of, fail

manteau.etymology: Manteau comes from Latin mantellum ('cloak, cloth covering') via Old French mantel; vocalisation of final -el before plural -s produced manteau (compare English 'mantle' and 'mantelpiece').

manuel.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–15th century from Classical Latin manualis ('belonging to or held in the hand') and Late Latin manuale ('small book that can be held in the hand', translating Greek enkheiridion), from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: done by hand, manual (adj.); textbook, handbook (noun)

marche.etymology: Combines two sources: (1) deverbal noun from marcher ('to walk, tread'), giving 'act of walking, military march, stair step (tread), operation of a machine'; and (2) Old French marche ('borderland, frontier'), from Frankish *marka ('boundary, borderland', cognate with English mark and march).

history.meaning: act of walking, pace, stair step, working order

marcher.etymology: Inherited from Old French marchier ('to trample underfoot, tread down, stamp'), borrowed from Frankish *markon ('to mark, impress with the foot, tread heavily', from *marka 'mark, footprint'); broadened in the 15th–16th century to 'to walk, go on foot' (replacing Old French aler a pié).

history.meaning: to leave a footprint, tread heavily
to trample -> to walk, march; (of a device) to work, function

marché.etymology: Inherited from Old French marchié ('marketplace, trade, commercial bargain'), from Classical Latin mercatus ('trade, traffic, marketplace, public fair'), derived from mercari ('to trade', from merx, mercis 'merchandise, wares').

history.meaning: open market, economic market, deal or bargain (bon marché)

mardi.etymology: Mardi continues Latin Martis dies, day of Mars. The twelfth-century French form marsdi preserves the older name more visibly.

marge.etymology: Adapted in Old and Middle French from Classical Latin margo, marginem ('edge, border, riverbank').

history.meaning: blank border of a page; leeway

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old/Middle French or directly from Latin marginem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marge

marge.notes: French school notebooks famously feature a red vertical line marking **la marge** on the left side of every squared page.

marin.etymology: Inherited/adapted in the 12th century from Classical Latin marinus ('of the sea'), derived from mare ('sea'); used both as an adjective ('marine, seagoing') and as a noun ('sailor, seaman').

history.meaning: of or belonging to the sea

marmite.etymology: From Middle French marmite ('deep lidded cooking pot'), substantivized feminine of Old French adjective marmite ('demure, secretive, hiding one's face'), humorously applied to a covered pot that conceals what simmers inside.

cognates.meaning: named after the French earthenware cooking pot pictured on its label

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marmite (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marmite

marmite.notes: In French home cooking, **faire bouillir la marmite** ('keep the soup pot boiling') idiomatically means 'to keep the household fed and running'.

marque.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 14th–15th century from marquer ('to mark, stamp'), borrowed via Old Occitan marcar / marca from Germanic *markon / *marka ('boundary sign, distinguishing stamp or brand').

history.meaning: distinguishing sign, brand, trademark, token, score

marron.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Franco-Provençal or Northern Italian marrone ('large cultivated sweet chestnut'), from a pre-Latin Alpine word *marra; used as an invariable color adjective ('chestnut-brown, brown') since the 18th century.

marteau.etymology: Inherited from Old French martel, from Late Latin martellus ('hammer'), diminutive of Imperial Latin martulus (an alteration of Classical Latin marculus 'small smith's hammer').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marteau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marteau

marteau.notes: Around 1709 Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the *gravicembalo col piano e forte* by replacing harpsichord plucks with tiny leather-and-felt **marteaux**.

massif.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from masse ('lump, mass, solid block', from Classical Latin massa < Ancient Greek maza 'barley cake, lump of dough') + adjectival suffix -if; used as a noun in geography and gardening for a mountain massif or flowerbed.

history.meaning: solid, heavy, bulky (adj.); mountain group, thick clump of shrubs (noun)

matin.etymology: Inherited from Old French matin ('morning'), from Classical Latin matutinum (sc. tempus, 'early morning hours'), neuter of matutinus ('of the early morning', derived from Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn, akin to maturus 'timely, early').

matinée.etymology: Formed in Old French (matinee, 12th c.) from matin ('morning') + suffix -ée denoting the full duration or activities of that part of the day.

history.meaning: the course or duration of the morning; afternoon theatrical performance

mauvais.etymology: Inherited from Old French malvais ('bad, wicked, worthless, cowardly'), from Vulgar Latin *malifatius ('ill-fated, born under a bad sign'), compound of Classical Latin malus ('bad') + fatum ('fate, destiny', parallel to Old Occitan malvatz).

me.etymology: Inherited from Old French me ('me, to me'), unstressed clitic development of Classical Latin me (accusative and ablative of ego 'I').

history.meaning: me, to me, myself (1st-person singular object pronoun)

meilleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French meillor ('better, best'), from Classical Latin meliorem (nominative melior, 'better'), synthetic comparative of bonus ('good').

mener.etymology: Inherited from Old French mener ('to lead, guide, drive'), from Late/Vulgar Latin minare ('to drive cattle onward with shouts and threats'), active reshaping of Classical Latin minari ('to threaten, jut out', from minae 'threats').

history.meaning: to drive animals with cries -> to lead, conduct
to lead, guide, direct, carry on

menthe.etymology: Inherited via Old French mente from Classical Latin mentha ('mint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek mínthē (in myth, the nymph Minthe transformed into the fragrant herb).

cognates.meaning: early West Germanic borrowing from Latin mentha

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menthe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menthe

menthe.notes: Hot green **thé à la menthe** steeped with fresh spearmint leaves is a beloved café staple across France.

menton.etymology: Inherited via Old French menton from Vulgar Latin *mentonem, enlarged from Classical Latin mentum ('chin', from an Indo-European root *men- 'to jut out', also seen in promontoire and éminent).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menton

menton.notes: Watch out for the look-alike verb **mentir** ('to tell a lie', from Latin *mentiri* 'to fabricate in the mind' < *mens*) — completely unrelated to **le menton**!

menu.etymology: Inherited from Old French menu ('small, fine, finely chopped, detailed'), from Classical Latin minutus ('made small, minute, petty', past participle of minuere 'to lessen, chop small'); as a noun (18th c.), originally the detailed list (le menu détail) of dishes to be served at a banquet, hence 'restaurant menu'.

history.meaning: slender, fine, minor (adj.); detailed bill of fare, menu (noun)

menuisier.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from menuise ('small work, fine craftsmanship', from menuiser 'to make small, carve fine details', from Vulgar Latin *minutiare < minutus 'small'); designated a craftsman working in small, finely fitted woodwork (joinery and cabinetry) as opposed to a heavy structural charpentier.

history.meaning: craftsman of fine fitted woodwork, joiner, carpenter

mer.etymology: Inherited from Old French mer ('the sea'), from Classical Latin mare ('sea', from PIE *mori 'body of salt water, marsh', cognate with English mere and German Meer).

merci.etymology: Merci comes from Latin merces, which meant pay or a price and later favour or grace. The Académie records ninth-century mercit with the sense of grace or mercy. Modern merci is the everyday expression of thanks; the older sense survives in sans merci.

history.meaning: pay, price; later favour or grace

merci.notes:
- Answer to *merci* is usually *de rien* or *je vous en prie*.
- *Non, merci* declines an offer; *Oui, merci* accepts it.

mercredi.etymology: Inherited from Old French mercresdi ('Wednesday'), from Vulgar Latin *Mercurii dies, transposition of Classical Latin dies Mercurii ('day of the god Mercury', translating Greek hemera Hermou).

merveilleux.etymology: Formed in Old French (merveillos, 11th–12th c.) from merveille ('wonder, marvel', from Vulgar Latin *mirabilia, neuter plural of Classical Latin mirabilis 'wonderful', from mirari 'to wonder at') + suffix -eux.

message.etymology: Inherited from Old French message ('errand, official communication; originally also the messenger himself'), from Medieval/Vulgar Latin *missaticum, derived from mittere, missum ('to send') + suffix -aticum.

history.meaning: that which is sent, mission, message
messenger -> spoken or written communication, message

mesure.etymology: Inherited from Old French mesure ('measurement, standard vessel, moderation, musical time'), from Classical Latin mensura ('a measuring, standard of measure, proportion'), derived from metiri, mensus ('to measure').

history.meaning: act or unit of measuring, proportion
measure, dimension, moderation, musical bar, step/action

mesurer.etymology: Inherited from Old French mesurer ('to ascertain the dimensions of, apportion, moderate'), from Late Latin mensurare ('to measure'), derived from Classical Latin mensura ('measure').

mettre.etymology: Inherited from Old French metre ('to put, place, set'), from Classical Latin mittere ('to send, let go, throw'); in Late and Popular Latin, mittere shifted from 'to send' to 'to put, place' (while Classical ponere narrowed to 'to lay eggs', French pondre).

history.meaning: to send, let go -> to put, place, set
to put, place, put on clothing, spend time

meuble.etymology: Shortened from biens meubles ('movable goods'), inherited from Spoken Latin *movibilis (Classical Latin mobilis, 'movable', from movere 'to move'). In medieval law property was either immeuble ('immovable': land and buildings) or meuble ('movable': chests, tables, beds).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: meuble (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: meuble

midi.etymology: Midi combines the older French elements mi, middle, and di, day. They descend from Latin medius and dies. The combination originally identifies the middle of the day.

miel.etymology: Miel comes directly from Latin mel ('honey'), with regular diphthongisation of stressed short e into ie (as in caelum -> ciel).

mien.etymology: Inherited from Old French mien ('mine, my own'), stressed tonic development of Classical Latin meum (accusative of meus 'my, mine', with the vowel modeling of tien / sien after tuum / suum).

history.meaning: mine (possessive pronoun); my own kin (les miens)

miette.etymology: Double diminutive formed in Old French from mie ('soft inner crumb of bread, tiny bit') + -ette, inherited from Classical Latin mica ('crumb, grain of salt, tiny morsel').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: miette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: miette

miette.notes: Modern French still distinguishes **la croûte** ('crust'), **la mie** ('soft inside of the loaf'), and **les miettes** ('loose crumbs').

mieux.etymology: Inherited from Old French mielz / mieus ('better, best'), from Classical Latin melius ('better'), neuter singular of melior used adverbially.

mijoter.etymology: Attested from Middle/Classical French in regional northern usage (originally 'to coddle, store fruit gently in straw or crumbs to ripen', then 'to cook very slowly over low heat'), expressive derivative built on Old French mie / Picard mijot.

history.meaning: to simmer slowly over gentle heat

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mijoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mijoter

mijoter.notes: Figuratively, **Qu'est-ce que vous mijotez?** means 'What scheme or surprise are you cooking up?'.

milieu.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (mi leu / milieu, 12th c.) of mi ('middle, half', from Classical Latin medius 'middle') + lieu ('place', from Classical Latin locus) — literally 'the middle place'.

history.meaning: middle place, center; social or natural environment

mille.etymology: The number mille was borrowed from Latin mille, thousand. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century; the number does not take an ordinary plural s.

millimètre.etymology: Coined in 1793–1795 as part of the French metric system from combining form milli- ('one-thousandth', from Classical Latin mille 'thousand') + mètre ('meter').

minuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French mienuit ('the middle of the night'), combining feminine mie (< Latin media 'middle') and nuit (< Latin noctem 'night'), exactly parallel to midi (< medius dies 'midday').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: minuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: minuit

minuit.notes: Originally feminine because *nuit* is feminine, **minuit** shifted to masculine on the model of **midi**.

minuscule.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–18th century from Classical Latin minusculus ('rather small, tiny', originally in paleography littera minuscula 'small cursive or lowercase script' as opposed to majuscula), double diminutive formed on minor, minus ('less, smaller').

minute.etymology: The time word minute comes from medieval Latin minuta, a noun use of the feminine of minutus, small. The Académie records it from the thirteenth century. The separate document-draft sense has its own specialised history.

minuteur.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from minuter ('to time to the minute, regulate duration', from minute 'sixtieth of an hour') + instrument suffix -eur.

miracle.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 11th–12th century from Classical Latin miraculum ('object of wonder, marvel; in Christian Latin, supernatural work of God'), derived from mirari ('to wonder at, marvel', from mirus 'wonderful').

miroir.etymology: Miroir comes from Old French mireor, built on mirer ('to look at, gaze at', from Latin mirari 'to wonder at, admire'). English 'mirror' was borrowed directly from Old French.
miroir.notes: **Regarder dans le miroir** = to look in the mirror.

moderne.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Late Latin modernus ('of the present time, recent, contemporary', coined in the late 5th c. from Classical Latin adverb modo 'just now, recently', on the model of hodiernus from hodie).

moi.etymology: Moi continues Latin me, me. The Académie records ninth-century French mi. It is the stressed object form rather than the subject form je.

moi-même.etymology: Compound intensive/reflexive pronoun formed from stressed pronoun moi ('me, I', from Latin me) + même ('self, same').

moineau.etymology: Diminutive in -eau (Old French moignel) of moine ('monk' < Late Latin monachus), affectionately naming the house sparrow after the brown-and-grey hood of its plumage, which reminded medieval observers of a friar's cowl.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: moineau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: moineau

moineau.notes: Older French called a sparrow **un passereau** (from Latin *passer*), which survives in **les passereaux** ('songbirds'), while cheeky little **moineau** ('little monk') won everyday speech!

moins.etymology: Inherited from Old French meins / moins ('less, fewer'), from Classical Latin minus ('less'), neuter comparative of parvus ('small', from root *mei- 'small, diminish').

mois.etymology: Inherited from Old French meis / mois ('month'), from Vulgar Latin *mense, Classical Latin mensem (nominative mensis, 'month', from PIE *meh1ns- 'moon, month', cognate with English month and moon).

moitié.etymology: Inherited from Old French meitié ('half'), from Classical Latin medietatem (nominative medietas, 'the middle, place in the middle, half', coined by Cicero from medius 'middle').

moment.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin momentum ('movement, impulse, small weight that turns the scale, brief particle of time'), contracted from *movimentum, derived from movere ('to move').

history.meaning: decisive weight on a scale -> brief span of time
moment, instant, short while; mechanical torque

mon.etymology: Mon and its feminine counterpart ma descend from Latin meus, mea and meum. The Académie records tenth-century mo. Modern forms agree with the possessed noun rather than naming the owner’s gender.

monde.etymology: Monde, world, descends from Latin mundus with the same meaning. It is recorded from the twelfth century. The rare adjective monde, clean, is a different dictionary entry.

monnaie.etymology: Inherited from Old French moneie ('coined money, mint'), from Classical Latin moneta ('mint, coined money', from the title of the goddess Juno Moneta on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, near whose temple the Roman mint was established).

monsieur.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French honorific form of address mon sieur ('my lord'), where sieur is a reduced proclitic form of seigneur ('lord, master'), from Classical Latin seniorem (comparative of senex 'old, elder').

montagne.etymology: Inherited from Old French montaigne ('mountain'), from Vulgar Latin *montanea ('mountainous region, mountain'), feminine noun from Late Latin montaneus ('of a mountain'), derived from Classical Latin mons, montis ('mountain').

monter.etymology: Monter comes from later Latin montare, to go up, derived from mons or montis, mountain. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century; riding and mounting are related extensions.

montre.etymology: Montre is a noun built from montrer ('to show, display', from Latin monstrare). It first named a shop display case and the visible dial that 'showed' the hours, before naming a pocket watch or wristwatch.

montrer.etymology: Inherited from Old French mostrer ('to show, point out'), from Classical Latin monstrare ('to point out, show, indicate, teach'), derived from monstrum ('divine omen, sign', from monere 'to warn, remind').

mortier.etymology: Inherited via Old French mortier from Classical Latin mortarium ('stone or wooden trough in which lime and sand — or kitchen herbs — are pounded together; the mortar mixed in it').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French mortier and Latin mortarium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mortier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mortier

mortier.notes: Just as in English, **un mortier** means both the mason's lime-and-sand mix between flagstones and the kitchen mortar used with a pestle (**un pilon**).

mot.etymology: Inherited from Old French mot ('utterance, speech, remark, word'), from Late/Vulgar Latin muttum ('grunt, murmur, uttered sound', as in non muttum facere 'not to utter a sound', from the expressive root of muttire 'to mutter, mumble'), which replaced Classical Latin verbum across Gallo-Romance.

moteur.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin motorem (nominative motor, 'one who moves, mover'), agent noun from movere, motum ('to move'); applied in the 19th century to mechanical engines.

history.meaning: prime mover, driving force (adj. & noun); mechanical engine, motor

motus.etymology: Playful 17th-century mock-Latin interjection built on French mot ('word' < Late Latin muttum 'muttered sound') + humorous Latinate ending -us, popularized in classical comedy for '(not a) word! hush!'.

history.meaning: not a word! mum's the word!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: motus (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: motus

motus.notes: Because of its mock-Latin disguise, the final *-s* of **motus** **/mɔtys/** is always pronounced aloud, especially in the beloved idiom **Motus et bouche cousue!** ('Mum's the word and lips sealed!').

mou.etymology: Inherited from Old French mol (feminine mole / molle, 'soft, yielding, weak'), from Classical Latin mollis ('pliable, supple, soft, gentle, weak', from PIE *mel- 'soft, crush').

mouillé.etymology: Past participle of mouiller ('to wet, soak, drench'), inherited from Old French moillier < Vulgar Latin *molliare ('to soften by soaking in water'), derived from Classical Latin mollis ('soft, supple').

history.meaning: to soften by steeping in water -> to wet

muet.etymology: Old French diminutive built on mu ('mute, silent', from Latin mutus) + -et. As one-syllable mu risked homophony in speech, the fuller form muet replaced it completely by Middle French.

cognates.meaning: silent (from Latin mutus / Old French muet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: muet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: muet

mug.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from English mug ('large cylindrical drinking cup with a handle, used without a saucer'), itself of Scandinavian origin (compare Swedish mugg, Norwegian mugge 'pitcher, mug').

history.meaning: large ceramic coffee or tea mug

municipal.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin municipalis ('belonging to a self-governing town or municipium'), derived from municipium ('free town whose citizens shared Roman civic duties', from munia 'public duties' + capere 'to take').

history.meaning: relating to a commune or town council, municipal

mur.etymology: Inherited from Old French mur ('stone or brick wall'), from Classical Latin murus ('city wall, defensive rampart, masonry wall').

muscle.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin musculus ('a muscle of the body; literally, a little mouse', diminutive of mus 'mouse', calquing Ancient Greek mys 'mouse; muscle', because the rippling of a flexed biceps under the skin resembled a mouse darting beneath a cloth).

musique.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French musique) from Classical Latin musica, from Ancient Greek mousike (sc. tekhne, 'the art of the Muses, encompassing poetry, song, and instrumental harmony'), derived from Mousa ('Muse').

mystère.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek mystḗrion ('secret rite, hidden truth'), derived from mýstēs ('initiate') and mýein ('to close the eyes or lips').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mystère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mystère

mystère.notes: Note the medieval homograph: Old French *mestier* ('craft, guild', modern **métier**, from Latin *ministerium*) was sometimes spelled *mystère* when craft guilds staged medieval 'mystery plays'!

mystérieux.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century from mystère ('religious mystery, hidden secret', from Latin mysterium < Ancient Greek mysterion 'secret rite of initiation', from myein 'to close the eyes or lips') + adjectival suffix -ieux.

mère.etymology: Inherited from Old French mere ('mother'), from Classical Latin matrem (nominative mater, 'mother', from PIE *meh2ter- 'mother', cognate with English mother).

mètre.etymology: Coined in 1791–1793 by the French Academy of Sciences (following Borda's proposal) as the fundamental unit of length of the decimal metric system, from Ancient Greek metron ('measure, rule, standard of length', which had already entered Old French for poetic meter).

history.meaning: poetic meter -> base unit of length in the metric system

mélodie.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin melodia from Ancient Greek melōidía ('singing, choral song, tune'), compounded from mélos ('limb; musical phrase') and ōidḗ ('song', source of ode).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mélodie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mélodie

mériter.etymology: Derived in Old French (meriter, 12th–13th c.) from mérite ('worth, reward, desert', from Classical Latin meritum 'that which is earned, service, reward', neuter past participle of merere / mereri 'to earn, deserve').

history.meaning: to earn, be worthy of, deserve

métal.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French metal) from Classical Latin metallum ('mine, quarry; mineral, metal'), from Ancient Greek metallon ('mine, quarry; ore, metal').

métallique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin metallicus ('of a mine or metal'), from Ancient Greek metallikos ('relating to mines or metals'), derived from metallon ('mine, metal').

history.meaning: made of or resembling metal, metallic

métier.etymology: Inherited from Old French mestier ('service, function, need, craft, guild'), from Vulgar Latin *misterium, contracted from Classical Latin ministerium ('office, service, attendance, occupation', derived from minister 'attendant, servant', learned doublet of ministère).

météo.etymology: 20th-century colloquial clipping of météorologie ('meteorology, weather forecasting', from Ancient Greek meteorologia 'study of phenomena high in the air', from meteoros 'raised on high, atmospheric').

history.meaning: study of atmospheric phenomena -> weather forecast or service

même.etymology: Inherited from Old French medisme / meïsme / mesme ('same, self, even'), from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, a superlative reinforcement of the emphatic pronoun phrase *-met ipse (as in egomet ipse 'I my very own self', combining intensive particle -met + ipse 'himself, very').

nappe.etymology: Nappe comes from Latin mappa ('napkin, signal cloth'), with dissimilation of initial m- to n- before -pp- in Popular Latin *nappa. English 'napkin' and 'apron' (originally 'a napron') both come from this French word!
nappe.notes: False friend: **la nappe** is a tablecloth; a napkin is **une serviette**.

naturel.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French naturel) from Classical Latin naturalis ('by birth, according to nature, innate'), derived from natura ('birth, inborn character, nature', from nasci, natus 'to be born').

naturellement.etymology: Formed in Old French (naturelment, 12th c.) from the adjective naturel ('natural') + adverbial suffix -ment.

ne.etymology: The negative ne continues Latin non. Its French history is recorded from the tenth century. The chemical abbreviation Ne belongs to an unrelated Greek-derived name.

nerveux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin nervosus ('sinewy, muscular, vigorous', from nervus 'sinew, tendon, bowstring, nerve'); shifted in modern medicine and everyday usage from 'muscular, sinewy' to 'relating to the nerves, high-strung, excitable'.

history.meaning: sinewy, wiry -> relating to the nervous system, tense, irritable

net.etymology: Inherited from Old French net ('clean, pure, spotless, clear'), from Classical Latin nitidus ('shining, bright, sleek, neat', from nitere 'to shine', cognate with English neat); reinforced in commercial senses ('net weight or price, free of deductions') by Italian netto.

neuf.etymology: Convergence of two distinct Latin words that became homophones in Old French: (1) the number neuf ('nine'), from Old French nuef < Classical Latin novem ('nine', from PIE *h1newn); and (2) the adjective neuf (feminine neuve, 'brand-new, newly made'), from Old French nuef < Classical Latin novus ('new', from PIE *newos).

neuvième.etymology: Formed in Old French (nuevieme, 12th c.) from neuf ('nine', using the voiced stem neuv- of neuve) + ordinal suffix -ième.

nez.etymology: Inherited from Old French nes ('nose'), from Classical Latin nasus / nasum ('nose', from PIE *nas- 'nose', cognate with English nose).

history.meaning: nose; sense of smell or flair

ni.etymology: Inherited from Old French ne / ni ('neither, nor'), from Vulgar Latin *nec, reduced from Classical Latin nec / neque ('and not, nor').

niche.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 13th–14th century from nichier / nicher ('to build a nest, nestle'), from Vulgar Latin *nidicare ('to make a nest'), derived from Classical Latin nidus ('nest', source of French nid); extended to an arched wall recess and a doghouse.

history.meaning: recess in a wall; doghouse, kennel

noir.etymology: Inherited from Old French neir / noir ('black, dark'), from Classical Latin nigrum (nominative niger, 'shining black, dark, sable'), which displaced ater across Romance.

nom.etymology: Inherited from Old French nom / non ('name, reputation, noun'), from Classical Latin nomen ('name, title, clan name, grammatical noun', from PIE *h1nomn- 'name', cognate with English name).

nommer.etymology: Inherited from Old French nomer ('to call by name, give a name to, appoint'), from Classical Latin nominare ('to name, call by name, nominate for office'), derived from nomen, nominis ('name').

history.meaning: to name, call, appoint to a post

non.etymology: Non continues Latin non. The Académie analyses the older Latin expression as *ne oinum, not a single one; the asterisk marks a reconstructed earlier form.

nord.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Anglo-Norman nort / nord) from Old English north ('the north', from Proto-Germanic *nurtha-).

nord-ouest.etymology: Compound compass noun formed in Old/Middle French from nord ('north') + ouest ('west', borrowed from Old English west).

normal.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from Classical Latin normalis ('made according to the carpenter's square, right-angled; conforming to a rule'), derived from norma ('carpenter's T-square, rule, pattern, standard').

history.meaning: conforming to the standard or rule, regular, normal

note.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin nota ('mark, sign, written character, musical symbol, marginal remark, brand'), related to noscere, notum ('to know').

history.meaning: musical note, brief written jotting, footnote, school grade, bill/check

noter.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin notare ('to mark, designate with a sign, write down, observe'), derived from nota ('mark, sign, note').

history.meaning: to write down, take note of, grade

notre.etymology: Notre comes from Latin noster, our. Ninth-century French had nostro. Modern plural nos belongs to this same possessive series.

nous.etymology: Nous descends from Latin nos, meaning we or us. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the ninth century. Modern nous still has both subject and object uses, so its history fits a wider range than the single English gloss we.

nouveau.etymology: Nouveau descends from Latin novellus, young or recent, itself related to novus, new. Twelfth-century French had novel; the alternative nouvel preserves that older shape.

nouvelle.etymology: The noun nouvelle, news, comes from Latin novella, a noun use of the neuter plural of novellus, new or recent. Its plural use for news should be distinguished from the adjective nouvelle and from the later literary sense short story.

noyer.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *nucarius ('walnut tree'), derived from Classical Latin nux, nucis ('nut, walnut'—which itself gave French noix). Like chêne or merisier, the tree name also names its timber.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: noyer (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: noyer

noyer.notes: An accidental homograph of the verb **noyer** ('to drown', from Latin *necare*), which has a completely separate origin.

nu.etymology: Inherited from Old French nu (feminine nue, 'naked, bare'), from Classical Latin nudus ('naked, bare, uncovered, stripped', from PIE *nogw-do-, cognate with English naked).

nuit.etymology: Nuit continues Latin nox, with the stem noct-. The Académie records tenth-century noit before the modern spelling.

numéro.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century (originally in merchant bookkeeping as an abbreviation N° written on bales of goods) from Italian numero ('assigned number in a series'), from Classical Latin numerus ('number', native doublet of nombre).

history.meaning: serial or identifying number, issue of a periodical, variety act

numéroter.etymology: Derived in the 17th–18th century from numéro ('serial number') + verbal suffix -ter (with linking -t- on the model of abricoter / chapeauter).

history.meaning: to assign sequential numbers to, number pages or items

nôtre.etymology: Inherited from Old French nostre ('our, ours'), from Vulgar Latin *nostrum for Classical Latin noster, nostrum ('our, ours', derived from nos 'we, us'); retains the circumflex accent (le nôtre) as a stressed tonic possessive pronoun.

objet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Scholastic Latin objectum ('something placed before the eyes or mind'), substantivized neuter past participle of Classical Latin objicere ('to throw or set before, present to sight', from ob- 'in front of, against' + jacere 'to throw').

history.meaning: that which is placed before the senses or mind
tangible thing, object; aim, subject matter

occasion.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin occasionem (nominative occasio, 'favorable moment, opportunity'), derived from occidere, occasum ('to fall down, happen, set', from ob- + cadere 'to fall').

history.meaning: favorable opportunity, occasion; bargain, secondhand item (d'occasion)

occupé.etymology: Past participle of occuper ('to take possession of, fill up space or time, keep busy'), borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin occupare ('to seize beforehand, take possession of, employ'), from ob- + capere ('to take, seize').

history.meaning: to seize hold of, fill, employ

octave.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Medieval Latin octava (sc. dies 'the eighth day after a church feast', or pars / consonance 'interval of eight diatonic degrees'), feminine of Classical Latin octavus ('eighth', from octo 'eight').

history.meaning: eight-day liturgical period; eight-note musical interval
musical interval of eight degrees, octave

odeur.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French odor / odeur) from Classical Latin odorem (nominative odor, 'smell, scent, fragrance, stench', from PIE *h3ed- 'to smell', cognate with Greek ozein and Latin olere).

officiel.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–18th century from Late Latin officialis ('relating to a public office or duty; magistrate's attendant'), derived from Classical Latin officium ('service, duty, public office', contracted from *opificium < opus 'work' + facere 'to do').

history.meaning: pertaining to an office or magistrate

officiellement.etymology: Formed in the late 18th century from the feminine adjective officielle ('official') + adverbial suffix -ment.

offrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French ofrir ('to present as a gift or religious offering'), from Vulgar Latin *offerire, remodeled from Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, offer'), compound of ob- ('toward, before') + ferre ('to carry, bring').

history.meaning: to offer, give as a gift

oh.etymology: Oh is an expressive interjection recorded in French from the sixteenth century. The Académie considers borrowing from the same Latin exclamation probable, rather than presenting that route as certain.

oignon.etymology: Inherited from Old French oignon, from Classical Latin unionem (accusative of unio, 'oneness, single large pearl; country Latin word for a single-bulb onion', contrasted with multi-clove garlic).

cognates.meaning: onion was borrowed from Old French oignon; union is its learned Latin doublet!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oignon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oignon

oignon.notes: Old French wrote *oign-* to represent palatal /ɲ/ after *o*; the 1990 spelling reform also permits **ognon** to match modern pronunciation /ɔɲɔ̃/.

oiseau.etymology: Inherited from Old French oisel ('bird'), from Late/Vulgar Latin aucellus ('little bird, bird'), diminutive formed on *auca (from Classical Latin avica, derived from avis 'bird'), which completely replaced Classical avis in Gallo-Romance and Italian (uccello).

olive.etymology: Inherited from Old French olive ('olive fruit, olive tree'), from Classical Latin oliva ('olive, olive tree'), borrowed from archaic Ancient Greek *elaiwa (Attic elaia, 'olive').

ombre.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin umbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Romance lowering of short Latin u to /o/ nasalised before m + consonant.

cognates.meaning: little shade (via Italian ombrello from Latin umbra)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ombre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ombre

on.etymology: On descends from Latin homo, meaning a human being. The Académie records om in the ninth century and hom or hum in the eleventh. A noun referring to a person became a subject pronoun; its older noun-like construction also explains l’on.
on.notes: The possessive can depend on the meaning: general on can go with son/sa/ses; when on means nous, notre/nos is common.

oncle.etymology: Inherited from Old French oncle ('uncle'), from Classical Latin avunculus ('mother's brother, maternal uncle', literally 'little grandfather', affectionate diminutive of avus 'grandfather'), which displaced paternal patruus across Romance.

onze.etymology: Inherited from Old French onze ('eleven'), from Vulgar Latin *undece, contracted from Classical Latin undecim ('eleven', compound of unus 'one' + decem 'ten').

or.etymology: Represents two converged Latin words: (1) noun or ('gold'), from Old French or < Classical Latin aurum ('gold'); and (2) conjunction/adverb or ('now, well now, whereas'), from Old French or / ore ('at this hour, now'), from Classical Latin hac hora ('at this hour').

orage.etymology: Inherited from Old French orage (originally 'strong wind, gust of air'), from Vulgar Latin *auraticum, built on Classical Latin aura ('breeze, breath of air', borrowed from Greek aúra).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orage

orage.notes: Unrelated to *or* ('gold')—its initial *or-* reflects Latin *au-* (*aura* -> *or-*), just as *aurum* gave *or*.

orange.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century (via Old Occitan auranja / Italian arancia, with blending of initial o- after French or 'gold' and the town name Orange) from Arabic naranj, from Persian narang, ultimately from Sanskrit naranga ('orange tree').

ordinateur.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin ordinatorem (nominative ordinator, 'one who puts in order, regulator', from ordinare); proposed in April 1955 by the Latinist Jacques Perret at the request of IBM France to translate English electronic computer ('a machine that puts information into systematic order').

history.meaning: one who arranges or puts in order

ordre.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (ordene -> ordre) from Classical Latin ordinem (nominative ordo, 'straight row, line of threads in a loom, rank, regularity, command').

history.meaning: order, tidiness, command, religious or chivalric order

oreille.etymology: Inherited from Classical/Colloquial Latin auricula ('earlobe, little ear'), diminutive of Classical Latin auris ('ear'). Across all Romance languages, spoken Latin preferred the expressive diminutive auricula over short auris.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oreille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oreille

oreille.notes: Adding *-er* to *oreille* produced **un oreiller**—literally 'the thing for your ear', i.e. a pillow!

oreiller.etymology: Inherited from Old French oreillier ('bed pillow'), derived from oreille ('ear', from Classical Latin auricula, diminutive of auris 'ear') + suffix -ier — literally 'that on which one rests one's ear'.

history.meaning: cushion for resting the ear/head, pillow

orientation.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from orienter ('to position facing the east or a compass point', from orient 'the east, point of sunrise' < Latin orientem, present participle of oriri 'to rise') + suffix -ation.

history.meaning: alignment with the points of the compass; direction, career guidance

origine.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin originem (nominative origo, 'birth, source, lineage, beginning'), derived from oriri ('to rise, spring forth, be born').

history.form: oriri ('to rise, spring up') -> origo, originem

orteil.etymology: Inherited from Old French arteil ('toe'), from Classical Latin articulus ('little joint, knuckle, digit'), whose initial vowel shifted from a- to o- in Gallo-Romance through the influence of Gaulish ordiga ('big toe').

cognates.meaning: learned doublet of orteil from Latin articulus

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orteil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orteil

orteil.notes: Few pairs look more surprising than **un orteil** ('a toe') and **un article** ('a newspaper article'), yet both trace back to Latin *articulus*!

oser.etymology: Inherited from Old French oser ('to dare, have the boldness to'), from Vulgar Latin *ausare ('to dare'), frequentative formed on the past participle ausus of Classical Latin audere ('to dare, venture', from avidus 'eager').

ou.etymology: Inherited from Old French o / ou ('or'), from Classical Latin aut ('or, either... or').

oublier.etymology: Inherited from Old French oblier ('to forget'), from Vulgar Latin *oblitare, frequentative built on Classical Latin oblivisci, oblitus ('to lose remembrance of, forget').

ouf.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection (attested since the 17th century) imitating a deep exhalation of breath upon being relieved from a burden, fear, or exhaustion.

ouh.etymology: Expressive vocalic interjection attested since Old/Middle French (ou / hou), imitating a hooting cry to express playful fright, teasing, booing, or chill.

history.meaning: expressive hoot of teasing, surprise, or shivering ('ooh!')

oui.etymology: Oui developed from Old French oïl, an affirmative response. The Académie dates the modern form to the fourteenth century.

oups.etymology: Modern expressive interjection (reinforced in the 20th century by English oops / whoops, alongside older French houp / hop) uttered upon making a slight slip, stumble, or mistake.

history.meaning: exclamation over a minor blunder or slip ('oops!')

outil.etymology: Inherited from Old French ostil / outil ('implement, working tool'), from Vulgar Latin *usitilium, altered (under the influence of uti, usus 'to use') from Classical Latin utensilia ('things for use, tools, utensils', neuter plural of utensilis).

ouvert.etymology: Ouvert is the past participle and adjective of ouvrir ('to open'), descending from Vulgar Latin *opertus (for Classical Latin apertus 'open, uncovered').
ouvert.notes: Feminine **ouverte** sounds the final t (/uvɛʁt/). English 'overt' was borrowed from Old French.

ouverture.etymology: Inherited from Old French overture ('opening, aperture, beginning'), from Vulgar Latin *apertura / *operitura, altered from Classical Latin apertura ('an opening', from aperire 'to open') under the influence of ovrir / ouvrir.

ouvrir.etymology: Ouvrir descends from Vulgar Latin *operire (a blend of Classical Latin aperire 'to open' with cooperire 'to cover', which gave couvrir). Intervocalic -p- voiced and softened to -v-.
ouvrir.notes: Conjugates like a -er verb in the singular present (*j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre*) despite its -ir infinitive; past participle **ouvert**.

où.etymology: Où descends from Latin ubi, where. The Académie records the French question word from the tenth century.

page.etymology: Represents two distinct words: (1) feminine la page ('side of a leaf of paper in a book'), borrowed in the 12th–15th century from Classical Latin pagina ('column of writing, leaf of papyrus; originally a trellis of vines', from pangere 'to fasten'); and (2) masculine le page ('young nobleman attending a knight or prince'), borrowed via Italian paggio from Medieval Greek paidion ('little boy', diminutive of pais 'child').

history.meaning: page of a book (f.); young court page (m.)

pain.etymology: Pain descends from Latin panis ('bread, loaf'). From Old French onward it has stood at the centre of daily meals and expressions such as gagner son pain ('to earn one's living') and copain (literally 'one who shares bread').

paire.etymology: Inherited from Old French paire ('matched set of two'), from Classical Latin paria ('equals, pairs'), neuter plural (reanalyzed as feminine singular) of the adjective par ('equal, matching').

paisible.etymology: Formed in Old French (paisible, 12th c.) from pais / paix ('peace', from Latin pacem) + adjectival suffix -ible.

history.meaning: inclined to peace, tranquil, peaceful, quiet

paix.etymology: Inherited from Old French pais ('peace, reconciliation, silence'), from Classical Latin pacem (nominative pax, 'peace, treaty, calm', related to pacisci 'to make a pact' and pangere 'to fix, fasten').

palier.etymology: Attested since the 14th–15th century ('level landing between flights of stairs'), probably derived from paille ('straw', from Latin palea, originally denoting a straw mat placed on a stair landing or the level floor of a granary); extended in modern French to a level plateau or stage.

history.meaning: stair landing; level stage or threshold, shaft bearing

panier.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin panarium ('breadbasket'), derived from panis ('bread', French pain) + -arium. Long after baskets came to carry everything at market, the word still preserves 'bread' at its core.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: panier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: panier

panique.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally in the adjective phrase terreur panique, Rabelais) via Latin panicus from Ancient Greek panikos ('of the god Pan'), because the ancients attributed sudden, groundless collective terror in lonely woods or armies to the woodland god Pan.

history.meaning: sudden terror inspired by the god Pan

paniquer.etymology: Formed in the 20th century from panique ('sudden fear, panic') + verbal suffix -er (reinforced by English to panic).

history.meaning: to be seized by panic, cause to panic

panne.etymology: Originated as a nautical term (mettre en panne, 17th c., 'to heave to, bring a sailing ship to a standstill by backing the sails'), from Old French panne / pene ('sail yard or upper corner of a sail; plush fabric or fur lining', from Latin penna 'feather, wing'); transferred around 1900 to the sudden breakdown or stalling of a motor vehicle.

history.meaning: to stop a ship by backing its sails
mechanical breakdown, power outage, fuel shortage

panneau.etymology: Inherited from Old French panel ('piece of cloth placed under a saddle, section of a net or wall'), from Vulgar Latin *pannellus, diminutive of Classical Latin pannus ('piece of cloth, garment, rag', source of French pan).

history.meaning: small piece of fabric, saddle pad
wooden wainscot panel, signboard, road sign, trap/snare

paperasse.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from papier ('paper') + pejorative/augmentative suffix -asse (modeled on Italian scartafaccio / carta).

history.meaning: waste paper, tedious red-tape documents, paperwork

papier.etymology: Papier comes via Latin papyrus from Ancient Greek pápyros ('Nile papyrus sedge, writing sheet'), shifting in the late Middle Ages to rag-and-pulp paper.

paquet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century (during the Anglo-Flemish wool trade) from Middle English paket / Middle Dutch pak ('small bundle or bale of wool or goods') + diminutive suffix -et.

par.etymology: Inherited from Old French par ('through, by, by means of'), from Classical Latin per ('through, across, during, by means of', partially blended in Gallo-Romance with pro).

par-dessus.etymology: Compound preposition and adverb formed in Old French from par ('through, over', < Latin per) + dessus ('on top, above', < de + sus < Latin sursum).

history.meaning: over, on top of, above and beyond

paragraphe.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–15th century via Medieval Latin paragraphus from Ancient Greek paragraphos (sc. gramme, 'short horizontal stroke drawn in the margin to mark a break in sense or change of speaker'), from para- ('beside') + graphein ('to write').

history.meaning: marginal stroke marking a new section of text
marginal symbol (§); distinct subdivision of a text, paragraph

parasite.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Classical Latin parasitus from Ancient Greek parasitos ('one who eats at another's table, sponger, flatterer in Greek comedy; originally a temple assistant who shared the sacred grain'), from para- ('beside') + sitos ('wheat, grain, food').

history.meaning: social freeloader; biological parasite (18th c.); static interference

paraître.etymology: Inherited from Old French pareir / paroistre ('to come into view, show oneself, seem'), from Vulgar Latin *parescere, inchoative form of Classical Latin parere ('to appear, be visible').

parce.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French (primarily in the causal conjunction parce que 'because') of the Old French phrase par ce (que) ('by this [fact that]'), from par ('by, through', < Latin per) + demonstrative pronoun ce ('this', < Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc).

pardon.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (pardon, 11th c.) from pardoner / pardonner ('to forgive, remit a debt or offense', from Late/Medieval Latin perdonare 'to give wholeheartedly, remit', from per- 'thoroughly' + donare 'to give').

history.meaning: forgiveness of an offense; polite apology ('excuse me, pardon')

parfait.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (parfit / parfait, 11th–12th c.) from Classical Latin perfectus ('completed, fully accomplished, flawless'), past participle of perficere ('to carry through to the end, complete', from per- 'thoroughly' + facere 'to make, do').

parfois.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French phrase par feiz / par fois ('by times, at times'), from par ('by', < Latin per) + fois ('time, occasion', < Classical Latin vicem 'turn, succession').

parfum.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from parfumer ('to scent by burning aromatic smoke').

history.meaning: aromatic smoke -> pleasant scent, perfume, culinary flavor

parfumer.etymology: Borrowed in the early 16th century from Old Occitan perfumar or Italian perfumare ('to fill with aromatic smoke, fumigate with incense or herbs'), compound of per- ('through and through') + fumare ('to smoke', from Latin fumus 'smoke').

history.meaning: to scent thoroughly with fragrant smoke

parler.etymology: Parler continues Christian Latin parabolare, to speak, related to parabola, speech. That word was borrowed from Greek parabolê, comparison or parable. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

parole.etymology: Inherited from Old French parole ('spoken word, speech, pledged word'), from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin parabola ('comparison, proverb, parable in the Gospels; hence speech, word'), borrowed from Ancient Greek parabole ('juxtaposition, comparison, parable'), which displaced Classical verbum in Western and Central Romance.

history.meaning: spoken word, faculty of speech, word of honor, song lyric

part.etymology: Inherited from Old French part ('portion, share, side, direction'), from Classical Latin partem (nominative pars, 'part, portion, share, side, party').

history.meaning: share, portion, side (quelque part, de la part de)

partager.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century from partage ('division into shares', formed in Old French from partir 'to divide into parts' + suffix -age).

history.meaning: to divide into shares, share with others

partir.etymology: Inherited from Old French partir ('to divide into parts, separate; reflexively se partir de, to separate oneself from a place, set out, leave'), from Vulgar Latin *partire, active reshaping of Classical Latin partiri ('to divide, share', derived from pars, partis 'part').

history.meaning: to divide -> to separate oneself, set out, leave, depart

partition.etymology: From Latin partitio ('division into parts', from partiri 'to divide'). In seventeenth-century music (matching Italian partitura), une partition meant dividing an ensemble piece onto aligned staves on one page so every voice or hand could be read together—hence 'musical score / sheet music'.

history.meaning: musical score arranged in aligned staves

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: partition (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: partition

partout.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French phrase par tot / par tout ('throughout all, in every place'), from par ('through, throughout', < Latin per) + tout ('all, everything', < Vulgar Latin *tottum).

pas.etymology: The negative pas began as the noun for a step, from Latin passus. It first strengthened negatives with movement verbs by referring to even a tiny distance, then became a general spoken negative marker.

passage.etymology: Formed in Old French (passage, 11th–12th c.) from passer ('to pass, cross over') + nominal suffix -age.

history.meaning: act or place of passing, crossing, corridor, excerpt of a text

passant.etymology: Present participle of passer ('to pass by, walk along'), used as a noun since Old/Middle French for a passerby on the street (or a belt loop through which a strap passes) and as an adjective ('busy with foot traffic', as in une rue passante).

history.meaning: passerby, belt loop (noun); busy with pedestrians (adj.)

passer.etymology: Passer comes from a reconstructed later Latin *passare, derived from passus, step. The Académie records the French verb from the eleventh century.

patiemment.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (paciement -> patiemment) from the adjective patient ('patient, enduring') + adverbial suffix -ment (with assimilation of -nt-m- to -mm-).

patience.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French pacience) from Classical Latin patientia ('quality of bearing or suffering calmly, endurance, forbearance'), derived from pati, patiens ('to suffer, endure, bear').

patrimoine.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin patrimonium ('inheritance passed down from a father', from pater, patris 'father'). Expanded in modern French from family estate to shared cultural and architectural heritage (le patrimoine historique).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: patrimoine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: patrimoine

patron.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin patronus ('protector of clients or freedmen, defender, advocate', derived from pater 'father'); evolved in Medieval and Modern French to mean 'patron saint', 'master of a ship or workshop, boss', and 'dressmaker's paper pattern (model)'.

history.meaning: patron saint; employer, boss, shop owner; paper sewing pattern

paume.etymology: Inherited from Old French paume, from Classical Latin palma ('palm of the hand; palm tree frond whose spread leaves resemble an open hand'), with regular vocalization of Latin -l- before -m-.

history.meaning: palm of the hand; palm branch

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French paume / Latin palma

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: paume (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: paume

paume.notes: Striking a ball with the bare **paume** gave medieval France **le jeu de paume** ('real/court tennis'), the direct ancestor of modern tennis.

pauvre.etymology: Inherited from Old French povre ('poor, destitute, unfortunate'), from Vulgar Latin *pauperus, 1st/2nd-declension remodeling of Classical Latin pauper ('producing little, poor, of small means', compound of paucus 'few, little' + parere 'to produce, bring forth').

pavé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of paver ('to pave with stones or tiles'), inherited from Old French paver ('to beat down earth or lay stones flat'), from Vulgar Latin *pavare, altered from Classical Latin pavire ('to beat, ram, tread down earth or pavement').

history.meaning: to lay a beaten or stone floor
cobblestone, paved street; thick heavy book or steak

payer.etymology: Inherited from Old French paier ('to appease, satisfy a creditor, pay'), from Classical Latin pacare ('to make peaceful, pacify, appease', derived from pax, pacis 'peace'); in Vulgar Latin, 'to pacify an angry creditor' came to mean 'to pay what is owed'.

history.meaning: to pacify, appease -> to satisfy a creditor

peindre.etymology: Inherited from Old French peindre ('to paint, depict in colors'), from Classical Latin pingere ('to embroider, tattoo, paint, adorn with color', from PIE *peyg- 'to mark, cut, paint').

peinture.etymology: Inherited from Old French peinture ('art or work of painting, pigment'), from Vulgar Latin *pinctura, altered (after the nasalized verb stem ping-) from Classical Latin pictura ('painting, picture', from pingere, pictum 'to paint').

pencher.etymology: Inherited from Old French penchier ('to tilt, incline, slope downward'), from Vulgar Latin *pendicare ('to hang down, incline'), frequentative of Classical Latin pendere ('to hang, be suspended').

history.meaning: to hang or slope toward one side

pendant.etymology: Originated in 13th–14th-century legal French as the present participle of pendre ('to hang, be suspended') in absolute constructions modeled on Scholastic Latin pendente lite / pendente processu ('while the lawsuit is hanging/pending, during the trial'), whence the general preposition pendant ('during').

history.meaning: while the case is pending -> during (prep.); matching counterpart or earring (noun)

penser.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in Early Old French (penser, 10th–11th c.) from Classical Latin pensare ('to weigh carefully, ponder, consider'), frequentative of pendere, pensum ('to weigh in the scales', native doublet of panser).

history.meaning: to weigh in the mind, ponder

pente.etymology: Deverbal/participial noun formed in Old/Middle French from pendre ('to hang down, slope', from Latin pendere), modeled on feminine past participles in -te (like vente, rente, tente).

perdre.etymology: Perdre descends from Latin perdere, originally to give wastefully and later to destroy or ruin. The Académie records the French verb from the ninth century.

permettre.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin permittere ('to let pass through, let go, give leave, allow'), compound of per- ('through') + mittere ('to let go, send').

history.meaning: to let pass through, grant leave

permission.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin permissionem (nominative permissio, 'a letting go, leave, authorization'), derived from permittere, permissum ('to allow, permit').

persil.etymology: Inherited via Old French perresil / persil from Late Latin petrosilinum, borrowed from Ancient Greek petrosélinon ('rock celery', compound of pétra 'rock' + sélinon 'celery, parsley').

cognates.meaning: blended from Old English petersilie and Old French perresil

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: persil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: persil

persil.notes: Greek **sélinon** in the second half of **persil** is also the exact source of French **céleri** ('celery')!

personne.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French persone) from Classical Latin persona ('actor's theatrical mask, dramatic character or role, legal individual', probably via Etruscan phersu 'masked figure'); through frequent use in negative sentences (ne... personne), also became the negative pronoun 'no one, nobody'.

history.meaning: theatrical mask -> dramatic role, human individual
person, individual (fem. noun); anyone / no one (pronoun)

petit.etymology: Petit is traced to a Gallo-Romance form *pit- expressing smallness. Medieval Latin pititus provides evidence for that family; the reconstructed base is marked with an asterisk.

petit-déjeuner.etymology: Modern French compound noun (19th c.) formed from petit ('small, light') + déjeuner ('breakfast, literally breaking the fast'); coined when urban déjeuner shifted from the morning meal to the midday lunch.

petit-fils.etymology: Compound kinship noun formed in the 16th–17th century (replacing Old French neveu in the sense 'grandson' after neveu narrowed to 'nephew') from petit ('little, younger') + fils ('son', from Latin filius).

peu.etymology: Peu continues Latin paucum, few or little. Early French spellings included pou, poi and po before peu became established.

peur.etymology: Inherited from Old French paor / peeur ('fear, dread'), from Classical Latin pavorem (nominative pavor, 'trembling, quaking, panic, dread'), derived from pavere ('to be struck with terror, quake with fear').

peut-être.etymology: Peut-être joins peut, the he/she present form of pouvoir, and être, to be. Twelfth-century expressions included put cel estre and puet estre; the hyphenated form is recorded in the seventeenth century.

pharmacie.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century via Late Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeia ('use or preparation of drugs, medicines, or potions'), derived from pharmakon ('medicinal herb, drug, remedy, poison').

history.meaning: science of preparing medicines; chemist's shop, pharmacy, medicine cabinet

pharmacien.etymology: Formed in Classical French from pharmacie ('apothecary art, pharmacy'), via Medieval Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('preparation of remedies'), from phármakon ('medicinal herb, remedy').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pharmacien (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pharmacien

pharmacien.notes: In 1777, a royal declaration in France officially established the *Collège de pharmacie*, replacing the older guild title **apothicaire** with **pharmacien**.

photo.etymology: Conversational clipping (attested since the second half of the 19th century) of photographie ('photography; photograph', coined in the 1830s from Ancient Greek phos, photos 'light' + graphein 'to draw, write').

phrase.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Late Latin phrasis from Ancient Greek phrasis ('way of speaking, diction, expression'), derived from phrazein ('to point out, declare, tell, express').

history.meaning: manner of speech, turn of phrase
turn of phrase -> grammatical sentence, musical phrase

physique.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (Old French fisique, originally 'natural science and the art of medicine') via Classical Latin physica from Ancient Greek physike (sc. episteme, 'knowledge of nature'), derived from physis ('nature, natural growth', from phyein 'to bring forth, grow').

history.meaning: physical (adj.); physics (fem. noun); bodily build or appearance (masc. noun)

piano.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Italian piano, both as a musical dynamic marking ('softly, quietly', from Latin planus 'flat, level, even, soft in sound') and as a clipping of pianoforte / forte-piano (invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence c. 1709 as gravicembalo col piano e forte 'harpsichord with soft and loud').

history.meaning: softly; keyboard instrument capable of playing both soft and loud

pic.etymology: Inherited from Old French pic ('iron pickaxe; sharp mountain peak; woodpecker'), from Vulgar Latin *piccus ('sharp point, woodpecker'), built on an expressive/pre-Latin root *pikk- ('to strike with a sharp point, peck').

history.meaning: pickaxe, sharp mountain peak, peak level, woodpecker

pied.etymology: Inherited from Old French piet / pié ('foot'), from Classical Latin pedem (nominative pes, 'foot; metrical foot; twelve-inch measure of length', from PIE *ped- 'foot', cognate with English foot).

history.meaning: anatomical foot, base or leg of furniture, plant stalk, foot measure

pierre.etymology: Pierre comes from Latin petra ('rock, stone', borrowed from Ancient Greek pétra). Diphthongisation of open e to ie and lenition of -tr- to -rr- yielded Old French piere, pierre.
pierre.notes: Also the source of the first name *Pierre* ('Peter'); **en pierre** = made of stone.

pile.etymology: Represents two Latin words that converged: (1) 'stack, heap, bridge pier, Voltaic battery (originally a stacked column of zinc and copper discs invented by Volta in 1800)', from Old French pile < Classical Latin pila ('stone pier, pillar'); and (2) 'reverse side of a coin; right on the dot (pile à l'heure)', from the medieval minting die pile ('under-iron').

history.meaning: masonry pier -> neat vertical stack, electric battery; coin face -> right on the dot

pince.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from pincier / pincer ('to pinch, grip tightly', from Vulgar Latin *pinctiare / expressive root *pints-).

history.meaning: gripping tool, pliers, tongs, tweezers, crab claw, dress dart

pinceau.etymology: Inherited from Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, a variant of Classical Latin penicillus ('painter's fine brush', originally 'little tuft of tail hair', double diminutive of penis 'tail').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French pincel (originally a fine camel-hair brush before graphite!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pinceau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pinceau

pinceau.notes: Watch the false friend: English *pencil* came from Old French *pincel*, but in modern French **un pinceau** is a paintbrush and **un crayon** is a pencil (and **penicillin** was named in Latin for its brush-shaped mold!).

pincée.etymology: Formed in Middle French from pincer ('to pinch between thumb and forefinger') + suffix -ée denoting the quantity held.

history.meaning: amount taken between two fingers, pinch (of salt, spice)

pire.etymology: Inherited from Old French pire ('worse, worst'), directly continuing the Classical Latin nominative singular pejor ('worse', synthetic comparative of malus 'bad'; the Latin accusative pejorem gave the archaic/literary French pis).

piste.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally in horsemanship) from Italian pista ('beaten track left by hooves, trail'), feminine participial noun of Late Latin pistare ('to pound, tread down', frequentative of pinsere).

history.meaning: trail, clue track, ski run, bike lane

cognates.meaning: pounded basil sauce (from the same Late Latin pistare!)
ski run or fencing strip, borrowed from French

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: piste (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: piste

piste.notes: **Une piste** ('trodden trail') and Italian **pesto** ('pounded sauce') come from the very same verb meaning 'to pound or tread down'!

pièce.etymology: Pièce is traced to reconstructed Gaulish *pettia, a small piece. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century. The theatre sense is one of several later uses of this general noun.

piège.etymology: Inherited from Old French piege ('snare that catches an animal by the foot'), from Late Latin pedica ('foot-snare, fetter, shackle'), derived from Classical Latin pes, pedis ('foot').

placard.etymology: Derived in the 15th century from plaquer ('to lay flat, plaster, post a bill on a wall', from Middle Dutch placken 'to patch, plaster, stick on'); evolved from 'posted wall bill' -> 'wooden door frame or paneling applied to a wall' -> 'built-in wall cupboard or closet'.

history.meaning: posted broadside, wall paneling -> built-in wall cupboard, closet

place.etymology: Place came through Latin platea from Greek plateia hodos, a broad street. The French noun is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern senses include a location, space or seat.

plafond.etymology: Originally spelled plat-fonds or plat fond in sixteenth-century architecture—literally 'flat bottom / flat underside' (plat 'flat' + fond 'bottom, background'), describing a flat boarded or plastered ceiling underside as opposed to an open arched vault. Fused into plafond in the seventeenth century.

history.meaning: flat underside of an upper floor

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: plafond (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: plafond

plaire.etymology: Plaire is a remodelling of the older French verb plaisir, itself descended from Latin placere, to be pleasing. The Académie dates plaire to the twelfth century.

plaisir.etymology: Inherited from Old French plaisir, originally the infinitive of the verb meaning 'to please, be agreeable' (modern plaire), from Classical Latin placere ('to please, seem good to'), substantivized as a masculine noun ('delight, enjoyment, favor').

plan.etymology: Plan blends two related Latin origins: planus ('flat, level surface', giving a flat architectural drawing or town map) and plantare ('to lay out on the ground'), expanding from a floor plan to any project or scheme.
plan.notes: **Un plan de la ville** = a city map; **un bon plan** = a good idea/deal.

planche.etymology: Inherited from Old French planche ('flat wooden board, footbridge'), from Late Latin planca ('flat board, slab', recorded by Palladius and Festus), related to Classical Latin plancus ('flat-footed') from PIE *plak- ('flat').

history.meaning: wooden plank, shelving board, engraved plate, garden bed

plancher.etymology: Derived in Old French (planchier, 12th c.) from planche ('wooden board, plank') + suffix -ier.

history.meaning: timber floor of a room, floorboards, ceiling structure; minimum floor level

plante.etymology: Represents two senses from the same Latin word: (1) 'sole of the foot' (la plante des pieds), inherited from Old French plante < Classical Latin planta ('sole of the foot, used to tamp down earth around a new shoot'); and (2) 'living vegetable organism, plant', borrowed in the 13th–16th century from Classical Latin planta ('sprout, slip, cutting, young plant').

history.meaning: sole of the foot; plant slip or shoot
sole of the foot; botanical plant

plaque.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 15th century from plaquer ('to apply a flat layer of metal, veneer, or plaster', borrowed from Middle Dutch placken 'to patch, stick on, plate').

history.meaning: thin flat sheet or plate of metal, stone, or glass; stovetop burner, badge, license plate

plaquette.etymology: Formed in the 15th century as a diminutive of plaque ('flat plate or slab') with suffix -ette.

history.meaning: small thin plate, slim brochure, blister pack of pills, brake pad, blood platelet

plastifier.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from plastique ('plastic') + causative suffix -fier (from Latin -ficare 'to make').

history.meaning: to coat or laminate with a protective sheet of plastic

plat.etymology: Inherited from Old French plat ('flat, level, even'), from Vulgar Latin *plattus ('flat'), borrowed from Ancient Greek platys ('broad, flat, level', from PIE *pleth2- 'flat, broad'); as a noun (un plat), denotes a flat serving dish and the course of food served on it.

history.meaning: flat (adj.); serving dish, prepared course of food (noun)

plateau.etymology: Inherited from Old French platel ('flat dish or platter'), diminutive formed from plat ('flat') + suffix -el (> -eau); extended in the 18th–20th century to a serving tray, an elevated flat tableland in geography, and a theater stage or film set.

history.meaning: flat platter -> serving tray, geographical plateau, stage/film set

plein.etymology: Inherited from Old French plein ('full, filled'), from Classical Latin plenus ('full, filled, complete', from PIE *pleh1- 'to fill', cognate with English full).

pleurer.etymology: Inherited from Old French plorer ('to weep, shed tears'), from Classical Latin plorare ('to cry out aloud, wail, lament; in Late Latin, to weep, shed tears', displacing Classical flere).

history.meaning: to wail aloud -> to weep, shed tears

pleuvoir.etymology: Inherited from Old French plovoir ('to rain'), from Vulgar Latin *plovere, 2nd/3rd-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latinimpersonal pluere ('to rain', from PIE *plew- 'to flow, pour').

pli.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (pli / ploi, 12th c., 'fold, crease, bend') from plier / ploier ('to fold, bend').

history.meaning: fold, crease, wrinkle; folded letter or envelope

pliant.etymology: Present participle of plier ('to fold, bend'), used as an adjective ('folding', as in une chaise pliante) and as a masculine noun for a folding camp stool.

history.meaning: pliable, folding (adj.); folding stool or chair (noun)

plier.etymology: Inherited from Old French pleier / plier ('to bend, bow, fold'), from Classical Latin plicare ('to fold, wind together, double up', from PIE *plek- 'to plait, fold').

plisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French plicier / plisser ('to gather into small folds, pleat, crease'), from Vulgar Latin *pliciare, derived from Classical Latin plicare, plicitum ('to fold').

history.meaning: to pleat fabric; to squint or crinkle (plisser les yeux)

pluie.etymology: Pluie comes from Popular Latin *ploia (for Classical Latin pluvia, 'rain', from pluere 'to rain'), matching Italian pioggia.
pluie.notes: Paired with the impersonal verb **pleuvoir** (*il pleut* = 'it is raining').

plus.etymology: Inherited from Old French plus ('more, most'), from Classical Latin plus ('more, in greater number or degree', comparative of multus 'much', which displaced magis in Gallo-Romance and Italian to form analytic comparatives).

history.meaning: more, most, plus; (with ne) no longer, no more

pluvieux.etymology: Inherited/adapted from Classical Latin pluviosus ('full of rain, rainy'), derived from pluvia ('rain', from pluere 'to rain').

poche.etymology: Inherited from Old French poche (Norman-Picard variant of Central Old French poque, 'bag, sack, pouch'), borrowed from Frankish *pokka ('bag, pouch', cognate with Old English pohha and English poke / pocket).

history.meaning: sack, pouch -> garment pocket, ladle, anatomical sac

pochette.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French as the diminutive of poche ('pouch, pocket') with suffix -ette.

history.meaning: small pouch, handbag/clutch, record sleeve, breast-pocket handkerchief

poids.etymology: Inherited from Old French peis / pois ('weight'), from Vulgar Latin pensum ('amount weighed out', neuter participle of pendere 'to hang on a scale, weigh'). Sixteenth-century humanists inserted a silent -d- in poids on the mistaken belief that it came from Latin pondus!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poids (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poids

poids.notes: From the same Latin *pensare* ('to weigh carefully') come both **peser** ('to weigh') and **penser** ('to think—to weigh in the mind')!

poignée.etymology: Formed in Old French (poigniee, 12th c., 'a handful; part of an object grasped in the fist') from poing ('fist, clenched hand', from Classical Latin pugnus) + suffix -ée.

history.meaning: handful; handle, doorknob, handshake (poignée de main)

point.etymology: Point descends from Latin punctum, a prick, tiny hole or dot, related to pungere, to prick. The Académie dates the noun to the eleventh century. Expressions such as au point extend the noun’s range.

pointe.etymology: Inherited from Old French pointe ('sharp tip, prick, headland, daybreak'), from Late/Vulgar Latin puncta ('sharp point, stab, prick'), feminine participial noun from Classical Latin pungere, punctum ('to prick, pierce').

history.meaning: sharp tip, tack/brad, headland, touch of spice or wit, peak hour (heure de pointe)

pointer.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from point ('dot, point, mark') and pointe ('sharp tip'); combines senses of 'to mark items on a list with a dot (check off), clock in at work', 'to aim a weapon or telescope toward a point', and 'to sprout or dawn'.

history.meaning: to check off on a list, clock in; to aim at a target; to appear

poli.etymology: Past participle of polir ('to make smooth and glossy, refine manners'), inherited from Old French polir < Classical Latin polire ('to smooth, polish, furbish, refine').
