pomme.etymology: Pomme comes from Late Latin poma (originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin pomum 'tree fruit', reinterpreted as a feminine singular). In French it narrowed specifically to the apple.

poncer.etymology: Derived from ponce ('pumice', in pierre ponce 'pumice stone', inherited from Latin pumicem). Before modern sandpaper, cabinetmakers smoothed wood and parchment by rubbing them with powdered pumice stone.

history.meaning: pumice -> to polish or smooth with pumice, then sandpaper

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poncer (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poncer

ponctualité.etymology: Formed in the 17th century from ponctuel ('exact to the point or appointed moment', from Medieval Latin punctualis < Latin punctum 'point, instant of time') + abstract noun suffix -ité.

history.meaning: scrupulous exactness in keeping an appointed time, punctuality

pont.etymology: Pont comes directly from Latin pons, pontis ('bridge'). Its accusative pontem regularly yielded Old French and modern French pont.
pont.notes: In French work life, **faire le pont** means taking a Friday or Monday off between a holiday and the weekend.

pop.etymology: Borrowed in the 1960s from English pop (clipping of popular in pop art and pop music), alongside native onomatopoeic uses imitating a light popping sound.

porcelaine.etymology: Borrowed via Italian porcellana (attested in Marco Polo's travels). In Italian porcellana first meant the smooth, glossy white cowrie shell (diminutive of porcella 'little sow', from a perceived shell shape); Europeans transferred the shell's name to translucent white Chinese ceramic with the same pearly lustre.

history.meaning: glossy white cowrie shell -> fine Chinese ceramic

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: porcelaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: porcelaine

porche.etymology: Inherited from Old French porche, from Classical Latin porticus ('colonnaded gallery, covered entrance porch'), derived from porta ('gate, entranceway').

cognates.meaning: porch was borrowed directly from Old French porche
learned doublet portique + base noun porte

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: porche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: porche

porche.notes: In French towns, **un porche** often names the deep vaulted stone carriageway leading from the street into a quiet inner courtyard (**la cour**).

portail.etymology: Inherited from Old French portal / portail ('monumental church doorway, main gate'), from Medieval Latin portale ('city gate, church porch, vestibule'), neuter noun derived from Classical Latin porta ('gate, entrance').

history.meaning: large entrance gate, church façade doorway
monumental doorway, carriage gate; internet web portal

porte.etymology: Porte comes directly from Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), sharing an Indo-European root for crossing or passing through with port ('harbour') and porter ('to carry').
porte.notes: Compare **le portail** ('large courtyard or driveway gate') from the same Latin family.

portefeuille.etymology: Compound noun formed in the 16th–17th century from verb stem porte- (from porter 'to carry') + feuille ('sheet of paper, leaf') — originally a stiff folding case for carrying loose sheets of paper or drawings, then a pocket wallet for banknotes and a minister's cabinet office.

history.meaning: case for loose sheets -> pocket wallet, investment portfolio, ministerial office

porter.etymology: Inherited from Old French porter ('to carry, bear, wear'), from Classical Latin portare ('to carry, convey, transport', from PIE *per- 'to lead across, carry', which displaced ferre across Romance).

portrait.etymology: Substantivized past participle of Old and Middle French portraire ('to draw forth, trace line by line, depict'), inherited from Classical Latin protrahere ('to draw forward, bring to light': pro- + trahere 'to draw').

history.meaning: to draw, depict -> drawn image, likeness

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old/Middle French portraire and portrait
drawn stroke or facial feature (from simple Latin trahere, tractum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: portrait (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: portrait

portrait.notes: Notice how **portrait** and **trait** share Latin *trahere* ('to draw a line'): hence the French idiom **tout le portrait de... / trait pour trait** ('the spitting image of...').

poser.etymology: Poser comes curiously from Late Latin pausare ('to pause, rest', from Greek paûsis 'cessation'), which in Romance took over the meanings of Classical Latin ponere ('to put, place') because of their similar past participles.
poser.notes: **Poser une valise** = to set down a suitcase; **poser une question** = to ask a question.

possible.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin possibilis ('that may be done or exist'), derived from posse ('to be able, can', compound of potis 'able, powerful' + esse 'to be').

postal.etymology: Derived in the mid-19th century (or borrowed via English postal) from poste ('mail service') + adjectival suffix -al.

history.meaning: relating to the mail or post office (carte postale, code postal)

poste.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Italian posta ('relay station where fresh horses are stationed along a road; mail courier service') and posto ('assigned place or station'), both from Vulgar Latin *posita / *positum, past participle of Classical Latin ponere ('to place, station').

history.meaning: station of relay horses; assigned position
mail service, post office (fem.); assigned station, job position, radio/TV set, extension (masc.)

pot.etymology: Inherited from Old French pot ('drinking vessel, cooking jar'), from Late Latin pottus ('drinking cup', recorded by Venantius Fortunatus in the 6th c.), of pre-Latin or Low Franconian origin (*pott).

history.meaning: pot, jar, flowerpot, exhaust muffler, friendly drink

poterie.etymology: Formed in twelfth-century Old French from potier ('potter', itself from pot + -ier) plus the craft/collective suffix -ie. English pottery was borrowed directly from Old French poterie.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poterie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poterie

poubelle.etymology: Eponym coined in Paris in 1884 (originally boîte Poubelle) after Eugène-René Poubelle (1831–1907), Prefect of the Seine, whose municipal decrees of 1883–1884 required Paris building owners to provide lidded waste containers for household refuse.

history.form: Eugène Poubelle (Prefect of the Seine) -> poubelle

pouce.etymology: Inherited via Old French polce from Classical Latin pollex, pollicem ('thumb, big toe').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pouce (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pouce

pouce.notes: Giving someone a gentle nudge forward with your thumb inspired **donner un coup de pouce** ('to lend a helping hand'), while playground truces cry **Pouce!** ('Time-out!').

poudre.etymology: Inherited via Old French polre -> poldre -> poudre (with regular glide consonant -d- inserted between -l- and -r-, followed by vocalization of -l- to -u-) from Classical Latin pulvis, pulverem ('dust, fine powder').

cognates.meaning: powder was borrowed directly from Old French poudre

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poudre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poudre

poudre.notes: In French baking, **sucre en poudre** is granulated/caster sugar (not icing sugar, which is **sucre glace**!), and **poudre d'amandes** is ground almonds.

pour.etymology: Pour continues Latin pro. The Académie records French pro in the ninth century, por and pur in the eleventh, and pour in the thirteenth.

pourquoi.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (por quei / pourquoi) of por / pour ('for', from Vulgar Latin *por < Classical Latin pro) + stressed interrogative pronoun quoi ('what', from Classical Latin quid).

history.meaning: for what reason, why (adv. & conj.); the reason why (noun)

pourtant.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (por tant, 'for so much, for that reason') of pour ('for') + tant ('so much', < Latin tantum); through frequent use in negative and concessive sentences, its meaning shifted in the 16th century from causal ('therefore') to adversative ('yet, nevertheless, however').

pousser.etymology: Inherited from Old Frencherd pouser / pousser ('to push, thrust, drive forward; to breathe heavily; to sprout'), from Classical Latin pulsare ('to beat, strike, knock, push forward'), frequentative of pellere, pulsum ('to drive, thrust').

history.meaning: to push, urge on; to utter a cry; (of plants or hair) to grow

poussière.etymology: Inherited from Old French poudriere / pousiere ('cloud of fine dust'), derived with collective suffix -ière from Old French pous ('fine dust, chaff'), which came from Vulgar Latin *pulvus for Classical Latin pulvis ('dust, powder').

poussiéreux.etymology: Formed in the 19th century (replacing older poudreux in everyday senses) from poussière ('dust') + adjectival suffix -eux.

poutre.etymology: Inherited from Old French poutre (originally 'filly, young mare', then by a vivid carpenter's metaphor 'heavy load-bearing timber beam', just as chevron 'rafter' came from chèvre 'goat' and chevalet 'trestle' from cheval 'horse'), from Vulgar Latin *pullitra ('filly'), derived from Classical Latin pullus ('young animal, foal').

history.meaning: filly -> heavy supporting beam or girder, gymnastics balance beam

pouvoir.etymology: Pouvoir descends from reconstructed Popular Latin *potere, a remodelling of Classical Latin posse, to be able. Earlier French forms included poeir before pouvoir became established.

premier.etymology: Inherited from Old French premier ('first'), from Classical Latin primarius ('of the first rank, chief, principal'), derived from primus ('first'), which displaced simple primus in Gallo-Romance.

prendre.etymology: Prendre comes from Latin prendere, a contracted form of prehendere, meaning to grasp or take. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. The idea of taking underlies its many extended senses.
prendre.notes: Very common: *prendre le petit-déjeuner*, *prendre une décision*, *prendre un bain*. Note the stem change: *il prend* but *ils prennent*.

presque.etymology: Presque developed from combinations involving the older French pres and que. The Académie records stages such as bien pres que and pres que before the words became the modern adverb.

presser.etymology: Inherited from Old French presser ('to squeeze, crush, crowd closely, urge on'), from Classical Latin pressare ('to press hard, squeeze'), frequentative of premere, pressum ('to press').

history.meaning: to squeeze (a lemon), press, hurry, urge

pression.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin pressionem (nominative pressio, 'act of pressing down, weight, leverage'), derived from premere, pressum ('to press').

history.meaning: physical or atmospheric pressure, moral pressure, snap fastener (bouton-pression), draft beer (bière pression)

pressé.etymology: Past participle of presser ('to squeeze, press; to hurry'), used as an adjective meaning both 'freshly squeezed' (citron pressé) and 'in a hurry, pressed for time'.

prier.etymology: Inherited from Old French preier / prier ('to ask earnestly, entreat, pray to God'), from Vulgar Latin *precare, active reshaping of Classical Latin precari ('to ask, beg, entreat, pray'), derived from prex, precis ('prayer, entreaty').

history.meaning: to pray; to beg, politely ask

principal.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French principal) from Classical Latin principalis ('first, original, chief, imperial'), derived from princeps, principis ('first in order, chief, leader', from primus 'first' + capere 'to take').

history.meaning: chief, main, principal (adj.); headmaster, principal sum (noun)

printemps.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *primum tempus ('first season, start of the fine weather', from primus 'first' + tempus 'time, season'), replacing Classical Latin ver. Fused in Old French as printens, later respelled printemps after temps.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: printemps (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: printemps

privé.etymology: Inherited/adapted in the 12th century from Classical Latin privatus ('set apart from public office, belonging to an individual, personal'), past participle of privare ('to strip, deprive; originally to separate as one's own', from privus 'single, one's own').

history.meaning: apart from the state, personal, private

prix.etymology: Inherited from Old French pris ('monetary value, worth, esteem, reward won in a contest'), from Classical Latin pretium ('worth, value, price, reward, wages'), giving both the commercial sense ('price') and the agonistic sense ('prize', which split into two words in English).

problème.etymology: Problème was borrowed through Latin problema from Greek problêma, something put forward and then a task or question. The French noun is recorded from the fourteenth century.

prochain.etymology: Prochain descends from reconstructed later Latin *propeanus, derived from prope, near. The French adjective is recorded from the twelfth century; its history connects next with nearness.

professeur.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin professorem (nominative professor, 'public teacher of an art or science'), agent noun from profiteri, professus ('to declare publicly, profess a calling or expertise', from pro- 'forth' + fateri 'to acknowledge, confess').

history.meaning: public declarer or teacher of a subject

progrès.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin progressus ('a going forward, advance, growth, improvement'), action noun from progredi ('to step forward, advance', from pro- 'forward' + gradi 'to step, walk').

prolonger.etymology: Inherited/adapted in the 12th–13th century (Old French prolongier) from Late Latin prolongare ('to lengthen, extend in space or time'), compound of pro- ('forward') + longus ('long').

history.meaning: to extend in time or length, prolong

promenade.etymology: Formed in the 16th century with suffix -ade from promener ('to take for a walk, walk back and forth'), earlier Old French pormener (por- 'forth' + mener 'to lead' < Late Latin minare 'to drive/lead onward').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: promenade (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: promenade

promenade.notes: **Une promenade** names both the act of strolling (**faire une promenade**) and the scenic tree-lined avenue itself.

promesse.etymology: Inherited from Old French promesse ('pledge, vow'), from Late/Vulgar Latin promissa ('a promise'), feminine singular reshaped from Classical Latin neuter plural promissa ('things promised'), past participle of promittere ('to send forth, foretell, promise').

promettre.etymology: Inherited from Old French prometre ('to pledge one's word, promise'), from Classical Latin promittere ('to let go forward, send forth; to give assurance, promise'), compound of pro- ('forth') + mittere ('to send').

history.meaning: to put forth -> to pledge, promise

prophétie.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French profecie) from Ecclesiastical Latin prophetia, from Ancient Greek propheteia ('gift of interpreting the will of the gods, prediction'), derived from prophetes ('spokesperson for a god, prophet', from pro- + phanai 'to speak').

proportion.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin proportionem (nominative proportio, coined by Cicero to translate Greek analogia from the phrase pro portione 'in accordance with each part's share').

propos.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (propos, 12th c., 'resolution, aim, subject of discussion, spoken remarks') from proposer ('to set forth, intend, propose').

history.meaning: purpose, subject at hand (à propos), spoken remarks

proposer.etymology: Proposer was borrowed from Latin proponere, to place before someone or set forth. Its French shape was influenced by poser. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

propre.etymology: Inherited from Old French propre ('belonging exclusively to someone, one's own, fitting, neat'), from Classical Latin proprius ('one's own, special, particular, characteristic'); in 16th–17th-century French, 'well-groomed, fitting' developed into the modern everyday sense 'clean, not dirty' (displacing net).

history.meaning: one's own (before noun); clean, tidy, literal (after noun)

propriétaire.etymology: Propriétaire comes from Late Latin proprietarius ('owner of property', from proprietas 'ownership', built on proprius 'one's own').
propriétaire.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine (**le / la propriétaire**).

protection.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Late Latin protectionem (nominative protectio, 'a covering over, shelter, defense'), derived from Classical Latin protegere, protectum ('to cover in front, roof over, shield').

protéger.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin protegere ('to cover in front, roof over, defend, shield'), compound of pro- ('in front of') + tegere ('to cover, roof').

history.meaning: to cover in front, shield from harm

près.etymology: Inherited from Old French pres ('near, close by'), from Classical Latin pressus ('pressed together, compact, close'), past participle of premere ('to press'), used adverbially in Late Latin (pressum 'closely').

précieux.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 11th–12th century (Old French precios) from Classical Latin pretiosus ('of great value, costly, dear'), derived from pretium ('price, worth, value').

history.meaning: valuable, precious; affected in speech or manner

précis.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin praecisus ('cut off short, abridged, brief, exact'), past participle of praecidere ('to cut off in front, cut short', from prae- 'before, in front' + caedere 'to cut').

history.meaning: strictly defined, exact, precise (adj.); concise summary textbook (noun)

préférer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin praeferre ('to carry in front, hold forth, place before in esteem, choose rather'), compound of prae- ('before, in front') + ferre ('to bear, carry').

history.meaning: to bear before -> to value more highly, prefer

préféré.etymology: Past participle of préférer ('to prefer'), used as an adjective and noun meaning 'favorite, best-liked'.

prénom.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally explaining the Roman praenomen) from Classical Latin praenomen ('first or personal name placed before the family clan name nomen'), compound of prae- ('before') + nomen ('name'); adopted during the French Revolution and modern civil registration to replace nom de baptême ('baptismal name').

history.meaning: fore-name placed before the family name

préparation.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin praeparationem (nominative praeparatio, 'a making ready beforehand'), derived from praeparare ('to prepare').

history.meaning: preparation, readiness, compounded medicine or culinary mixture

préparer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin praeparare ('to make ready beforehand, equip, fit out'), compound of prae- ('beforehand') + parare ('to make ready, procure').

prévoir.etymology: Formed in the 13th–15th century (remodeling Old French porveoir after Latin praevidere) from prefix pré- (Latin prae- 'beforehand') + voir ('to see', from Latin videre).

history.meaning: to see beforehand, foresee, plan for

prêt.etymology: Represents two related words: (1) adjective prêt ('ready, prepared'), inherited from Old French prest < Late Latin praestus ('at hand, ready, prompt', from Classical adverb praesto 'here, at hand'); and (2) masculine noun un prêt ('a loan'), deverbal from prêter ('to lend', from Classical Latin praestare 'to stand surety for, furnish, lend').

history.meaning: at hand, ready; to furnish or lend
ready (adj.); loan of money or goods (noun)

public.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin publicus ('pertaining to the people or state, common, open to all', altered from Old Latin poplicus under the influence of pubes 'adult population', from populus 'people').

history.meaning: of the people or state, open to all

puis.etymology: Inherited from Old French puis ('afterward, next, then'), from Vulgar Latin *postius, comparative adverb built on Classical Latin post ('behind, after').

pull.etymology: 20th-century clipping of pull-over ('knitted sweater pulled on over the head'), borrowed in the 1920s from English pullover (from pull + over).

pupitre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (pupiltre -> pupitre) from Classical Latin pulpitum ('wooden platform, reading stand, lectern'—the same Latin word that gave English pulpit).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pupitre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pupitre

pur.etymology: Inherited from Old French pur ('unmixed, clean, spotless, sheer'), from Classical Latin purus ('clean, free from dirt or admixture, chaste, plain', from PIE *pewH- 'to cleanse, purify').

pâle.etymology: Inherited from Old French pale / pasle ('wan, pallid, light-colored'), from Classical Latin pallidus ('pale, wan, colorless', derived from pallere 'to be pale', with an unetymological s inserted in Middle French that left the circumflex accent).

pâlir.etymology: Formed in Old French (palir, 12th c.) from the adjective pale / pâle ('pale') + inchoative suffix -ir (continuing Latin pallescere).

history.meaning: to turn pale, grow dim or fade

pâte.etymology: Inherited from Old French paste ('dough, kneaded mixture'), from Late Latin pasta ('dough, medicinal lozenge, paste'), borrowed from Ancient Greek paste ('barley porridge or salted mess of flour and sauce', from passein 'to sprinkle with salt').

pâtisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French pasticier ('to knead dough, make pies and pastries'), from Vulgar Latin *pasticiare, derived from Late Latin pasta ('dough').

pâté.etymology: Inherited from Old French pasté ('meat or fish baked inside a pastry crust'), participial noun from pasteler / pâte ('dough', < Late Latin *pastatum); later extended to the seasoned minced meat mixture itself even when cooked in a terrine without crust, as well as a child's sandcastle (pâté de sable) or inkblot.

history.meaning: savory dish baked in a pastry crust
meat pie, savory meat spread (pâté), block of houses, sandcastle, inkblot

pédale.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century (originally for the foot-keys of a pipe organ) from Italian pedale ('organ foot-lever'), substantivized from Classical Latin pedalis ('of the foot, a foot long'), derived from pes, pedis ('foot'); extended in the 19th century to piano, sewing-machine, and bicycle pedals.

history.meaning: organ, piano, bicycle, or automobile foot pedal

pénible.etymology: Pénible is derived from peine, trouble or effort. The Académie dates the adjective to the twelfth century. It is not explained by simply assigning a generic meaning to the ending -ible.

pétrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French pestrir ('to knead dough'), from Late/Vulgar Latin *pisturire, built on Classical Latin pistura ('pounding grain, baking') and pistor ('baker', originally 'grain-pounder', from pinsere 'to crush, knead').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pétrir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pétrir

pétrir.notes: The wooden kneading trough in a traditional French bakery is called **le pétrin** (whence the idiom *être dans le pétrin*, 'to be in a sticky jam').

qu'est-ce.etymology: Qu'est-ce contracts que ('what', from Latin quid) + est ('is', from Latin est) + ce ('that/it', from Latin ecce hoc), forming the standard spoken French opening for 'what' questions (*qu'est-ce qui*, *qu'est-ce que*).
qu'est-ce.notes: Pronounced /kɛs/ as a single smooth syllable before *qui* or *que*.

qu'est-ce que.etymology: This question expression combines interrogative que, the verb est and the demonstrative ce, followed by que. The Académie treats the interrogative construction under que. Its pieces became a familiar way to introduce a question about an object.

quai.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Norman-Picard cai / quai ('earth embankment, stone wharf along a river or harbor', corresponding to Central Old French chai 'wine cellar'), from Gaulish *kagion ('hedge, wattled enclosure, retaining bank', cognate with Welsh cae 'enclosure, hedge').

history.meaning: stone embankment, harbor quay, railway station platform

quand.etymology: Quand continues Latin quando, when. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.

quarante.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarante ('forty'), from Vulgar Latin *quarranta, contracted from Classical Latin quadraginta ('forty', derived from quattuor 'four').

quarante-quatre.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from quarante ('forty') + quatre ('four').

quart.etymology: Inherited from Old French quart ('fourth; a fourth part, quarter'), from Classical Latin quartus ('fourth', ordinal of quattuor 'four').

history.meaning: one-fourth, quarter (of an hour, pound, etc.); sailor's watch

quartier.etymology: Inherited from Old French quartier ('one-fourth part of something divided in four; one of the four administrative wards of a town; military camp quarters'), from Classical Latin quartarius ('fourth part of a measure, gill'), derived from quartus ('fourth').

history.meaning: quarter slice (of fruit or moon), city neighborhood/district, military quarters

quatorze.etymology: Quatorze descends from Latin quattuordecim, built from the words for four and ten. It is recorded in French from the twelfth century.

quatre.etymology: Inherited from Old French quatre ('four'), from Vulgar Latin *quattor for Classical Latin quattuor ('four', from PIE *kwetwores, cognate with English four).

quatre-vingts.etymology: Inherited from Old French quatre vinz ('four twenties, eighty'), a vestige of the vigesimal (base-20) counting system widespread in medieval French (which also produced l'hôpital des Quinze-Vingts '300' and formerly six-vingts '120'), often attributed to Gaulish/Celtic or Norman substrate influence.

quatrième.etymology: Formed in Old French (quatrieme, 12th–13th c., gradually replacing older ordinal quart) from quatre ('four') + ordinal suffix -ième.

que.etymology: Several older words converged in French que. Interrogative que continues Latin quid; relative que continues quem; the connecting conjunction developed from quia. These histories help explain why one spelling has different grammatical jobs.

quel.etymology: Quel descends from Latin qualis, of what kind or nature. The Académie records the French word from the tenth century.

quelqu'un.etymology: Quelqu’un combines the indefinite quelque and un. The Académie records the compound from the thirteenth century. The apostrophe marks the joining of these two pieces.

quelque.etymology: Quelque was formed from quel and the conjunction que. The Académie records the combination from the eleventh century.

question.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin quaestionem (nominative quaestio, 'a seeking, inquiry, judicial investigation, subject of debate'), derived from quaerere, quaesitum ('to seek, ask, inquire').

qui.etymology: Relative qui continues Latin qui, while interrogative qui continues Latin quis. The Académie records the relative in the ninth century and the question word in the tenth; their modern spellings coincide.

quincaillerie.etymology: Formed in the 17th century (by assimilation of initial c- to qu- from earlier clincaillerie, 16th c.) from clincaille / quincaille ('small clinking articles of iron, copper, or tinware'), derived from Middle Dutch klinken ('to clink, ring, jingle', cognate with English clink).

history.meaning: jingle of small metal wares -> hardware, hardware store

quinze.etymology: Inherited from Old French quinze ('fifteen'), from Vulgar Latin *quindece, contracted from Classical Latin quindecim ('fifteen', compound of quinque 'five' + decem 'ten').

quoi.etymology: Quoi is the stressed descendant of Latin quid ('what?'), where Latin short i opened to e and diphthongised in stressed position through ei and oi to /kwa/.
quoi.notes: Used after prepositions (*avec quoi?*, *de quoi?*) or at the end of spoken questions (*C'était quoi?*).

rabat.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from rabattre ('to beat or fold back down, turn down, deduct from a price'); denotes a folded-down collar, clerical bands, or the top flap of an envelope, pocket, or binder.

history.meaning: folding flap (of an envelope or pocket), turned-down collar

raccourci.etymology: Substantivized past participle (16th–17th century) of raccourcir ('to shorten': re- + accourcir, built on court 'short' < Classical Latin curtus).

cognates.meaning: from Latin curtus and Middle French courtault

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: raccourci (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: raccourci

raccourci.notes: Today **un raccourci** means both a cobbled alley shortcut (**prendre un raccourci**) and a keyboard shortcut (**un raccourci clavier**).

raccrocher.etymology: Formed in Middle French from iterative prefix r- / re- ('again, back') + accrocher ('to hang on a hook', from croc 'hook'); acquired the modern sense 'to hang up the telephone receiver' from hanging the earpiece back on its switchhook.

history.meaning: to hang back on a hook -> to hang up the phone

raconter.etymology: Formed in Old French (raconter, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- + aconter ('to count up, reckon, relate in detail', from à + conter < Classical Latin computare 'to reckon, recount').

history.meaning: to recount in detail, narrate, tell a story

radiateur.etymology: Formed in the mid-19th century by French physicists and engineers from the stem of radier ('to radiate heat or light', from Classical Latin radiare < radius 'ray, spoke') + instrument suffix -teur.

history.meaning: heat-radiating heating unit or engine cooling radiator

raison.etymology: Inherited from Old French raison ('reckoning, account, faculty of thought, argument, justice, speech'), from Classical Latin rationem (nominative ratio, 'reckoning, calculation, account, faculty of judgment, motive', derived from reri, ratus 'to reckon, think').

history.meaning: faculty of reason, good sense, motive, rightness (avoir raison)

rallumer.etymology: Formed in Old French (ralumer, 12th c.) from iterative prefix r- / re- ('again') + allumer ('to light, kindle').

history.meaning: to relight, rekindle, switch back on

ramener.etymology: Formed in Old French (ramener, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + amener ('to bring, lead toward').

history.meaning: to bring back, lead back, restore

rang.etymology: Inherited from Old French renc ('circle of spectators or combatants, row, line of soldiers'), borrowed from Frankish *hring ('ring, circle, assembly of warriors or judges standing in a circle', cognate with English ring).

history.meaning: circle, ring of men gathered for battle or council
circle -> line, row, tier, social rank

ranger.etymology: Derived in Old French (rengier, 12th c., 'to draw up troops in battle lines, arrange in rows') from renc / rang ('row, line, rank').

history.meaning: to line up in rows -> to put in order, tidy away, park

rapide.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–17th century from Classical Latin rapidus ('tearing away, rushing, swift, impetuous', originally describing a torrent or fire), derived from rapere ('to seize, snatch, carry off').

history.meaning: fast, swift, rapid (adj.); river rapids, express train (noun)

rappeler.etymology: Rappeler is a French derivative of appeler. The Académie records it from the eleventh century. The additional beginning can contribute the sense of calling again or calling back.

rapporter.etymology: Formed in Old French (raporter, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + apporter ('to bring, carry to').

history.meaning: to bring back, yield profit, report, tell on

rassembler.etymology: Formed in Old French (rasembler, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('together, again') + assembler ('to bring together', from Vulgar Latin *assimulare < ad + simul 'together').

history.meaning: to gather together, collect, reassemble, summon up

rassurer.etymology: Formed in Old French (rasseürer, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- + assurer ('to make secure, give confidence', from Vulgar Latin *assecurare < securus 'free from care, safe').

history.meaning: to restore confidence to, calm someone's fears, reassure

rater.etymology: Attested from the 16th–17th century; originally meant 'to be eaten by rats' or (in hunting/firearms, prendre un rat) 'to misfire, fail to go off' (comparing a flintlock that clicks without firing to a trap that snaps without catching a rat), whence 'to miss a target, fail an exam, miss a train'.

history.meaning: to misfire (of a gun) -> to miss, fail, bungle

ravi.etymology: Past participle of ravir ('to snatch away by force, carry off to heaven in ecstasy, delight'), inherited from Old French ravir < Vulgar Latin *rapire for Classical Latin rapere ('to seize, carry off').

history.meaning: carried away with joy, delighted, thrilled

rayure.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from rayer ('to scratch with a line, stripe, strike out', from raie 'furrow, line, stripe' < Gallo-Romance *rica 'furrow') + nominal suffix -ure.

history.meaning: decorative stripe, scratch on glass or metal, rifling groove

rebonjour.etymology: Colloquial modern French greeting formed from iterative prefix re- ('again') + bonjour ('hello, good day'), used when seeing the same person a second time in the same day.

rebord.etymology: Formed in the 15th century from prefix re- ('turned back, projecting') + bord ('edge, rim').

history.meaning: raised or folded rim, ledge, windowsill, lapel/brim

rebours.etymology: From Old French rebors ('bristling the wrong way, contrary'), inherited from Late Latin reburrus ('with hair standing up backward', from re- 'back' + burra 'shaggy wool, coarse nap'). Brushing cloth or fur à rebours meant stroking it against the grain—hence 'in reverse' and un compte à rebours ('countdown').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: rebours (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: rebours

recette.etymology: Inherited via Old French receite ('money or goods received; medical/culinary formula') from Medieval Latin recepta, substantivized feminine/neuter plural of Classical Latin receptus (from recipere 'to receive, take'), echoing the apothecary heading Recipe ('Take...').

history.meaning: to take, receive -> things received; formula

cognates.meaning: receipt came from Anglo-Norman receite (note old cookbooks called recipes 'receipts'!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: recette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: recette

recette.notes: **Une recette** still keeps both historical meanings in French: **une recette de cuisine** ('a recipe') and **les recettes** ('box-office or shop takings').

recevoir.etymology: Inherited from Old French receivre / recevoir ('to take in, welcome, receive'), from Classical Latin recipere ('to take back, take to oneself, admit, receive'), compound of re- + capere ('to take').

rechange.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (rechange, 12th–13th c.) from rechangier ('to exchange again, replace'); preserved chiefly in the phrase de rechange ('spare, replacement', as in une roue de rechange 'spare tire', des vêtements de rechange).

history.meaning: replacement, spare part or change of clothes

recommander.etymology: Formed in Old French (recomander, 12th c.) from prefix re- + comander / commander ('to entrust to someone's care, commend'); in postal usage (recommander une lettre), means to register a letter for tracked, guaranteed delivery.

history.meaning: to entrust to someone's favor, speak in favor of, advise; to register mail

recommandé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of recommander (supplying envoi or pli recommandé, 'registered mail item'), attested since the 19th century.

reconnaître.etymology: Inherited from Old French reconoistre ('to identify again, acknowledge, explore'), from Classical Latin recognoscere ('to know again, recall to mind, examine, certify'), compound of re- ('again') + cognoscere ('to come to know').

reculer.etymology: Formed in Old French (reculer, 12th c., 'to move backward, draw back') from prefix re- ('back') + cul ('backside, rear end, bottom', from Classical Latin culus) + verbal ending -er.

history.meaning: to move tail-first, step backward, retreat, postpone

redonner.etymology: Formed in Old French (redoner, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + donner ('to give').

history.meaning: to give back, restore, give again

redresser.etymology: Formed in Old French (redrecier, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + dresser ('to set upright, straighten', from Vulgar Latin *directiare < directus 'straight').

history.meaning: to set upright again, straighten out, right a wrong

refermer.etymology: Formed in Old French (refermer, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, back') + fermer ('to close, shut').

reflet.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 17th century (originally in painting science, translating Italian riflesso) from refléter ('to throw back light or color', itself an alteration of réfléchir < Classical Latin reflectere 'to bend or turn back').

history.meaning: reflected gleam of light, glint, mirror image

refroidir.etymology: Formed in Old French (refroidir, 12th c.) from prefix re- + froidir / froid ('cold', from Vulgar Latin *frigidus for Classical frigidus).

history.meaning: to make or become cold again, cool down, chill

refuser.etymology: Inherited from Old French refuser ('to reject, decline'), from Vulgar Latin *refusare, frequentative built on the past participle refusus of Classical Latin refundere ('to pour back, give back, reject, spurn') blended with recusare ('to refuse, object to').

history.meaning: to pour or push back, reject

regarder.etymology: Regarder was formed in Old French from re- + garder ('to watch, guard', from Frankish *wardon 'to keep watch', cognate with English 'ward' and 'regard').
regarder.notes: No preposition for 'at': **regarder l'étiquette** = 'to look at the label'.

registre.etymology: Inherited from Old French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum, an alteration of Late Latin regesta ('matters recorded or entered in a book', neuter plural past participle of regerere 'to carry back, transcribe').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: registre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: registre

registre.notes: From organ stops (**tirer les registres**), **le registre** also entered music and linguistics to mean vocal range or tone of speech (`tu` vs `vous`).

rejoindre.etymology: Formed in Old French (rejoindre, 12th–13th c.) from prefix re- ('together again, back') + joindre ('to join', from Classical Latin jungere).

history.meaning: to join together again, reunite with, catch up with, meet

relever.etymology: Inherited from Old French relever ('to raise up again, relieve a feudal tenant or sentry'), from Classical Latin relevare ('to lift up again, lighten, alleviate'), compound of re- ('again, up') + levare ('to lift').

history.meaning: to raise up again, turn up, note down (a meter), spice up food, relieve on watch

relire.etymology: Formed in Old French (relire, 12th c.) from iterative prefix re- ('again') + lire ('to read', from Latin legere).

remboursement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from rembourser ('to put money back into someone's purse, repay', from re- + embourser, built on bourse 'purse') + nominal suffix -ment.

remercier.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from prefix re- + mercier ('to thank', derived from Old French merci 'favor, grace, thanks' < Classical Latin mercedem 'reward, wages, favor').

history.meaning: to express gratitude to, thank; (euphemistically) to dismiss an employee

remettre.etymology: Inherited from Old French remetre ('to put back in place, hand over, postpone, forgive'), from Classical Latin remittere ('to send back, slacken, give up, forgive'), compound of re- ('back, again') + mittere ('to send; in Romance, to put').

history.meaning: to put back, hand over/deliver, put on again, postpone, recognize

remonter.etymology: Formed in Old French (remonter, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('up again, back') + monter ('to go up, mount, assemble').

history.meaning: to go back up, wind a clock, reassemble, trace back in time, cheer up

remplir.etymology: Formed in Old French (raemplir -> remplir, 11th–12th c.) from intensive/iterative prefix re- + emplir ('to fill', from Classical Latin implere 'to fill up').

history.meaning: to fill up completely, refill, fulfill a duty, fill out a form

remuer.etymology: Formed in Old French (remuer, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, thoroughly') + muer ('to change, move, shift', from Classical Latin mutare 'to change, move').

history.meaning: to move about, stir, shake, fidget

rencontrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (rencontrer, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- + encontrer ('to meet face to face, come upon', from Late Latin incontrare, derived from in + contra 'against, facing').

history.meaning: to come upon face to face, meet, encounter

rendez-vous.etymology: Rendez-vous began as an instruction: the polite or plural imperative of se rendre. The Académie records the expression used as a noun from the sixteenth century.

rendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French rendre ('to give back, hand over, yield'), from Vulgar Latin *rendere, nasalized alteration (under the influence of prendre 'to take') of Classical Latin reddere ('to give back, return, restore', from red- 'back' + dare 'to give').

history.meaning: to give back, return, yield, make (+ adj.)

rentrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (rentrer, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + entrer ('to go in, enter').

history.meaning: to go or come back in, return home, resume school after vacation, bring inside

renverser.etymology: Formed in Old French (renverser, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- + enverser ('to turn upside down, throw on one's back', derived from envers < Classical Latin inversus 'turned upside down').

history.meaning: to knock over, spill, overturn, reverse

renvoyer.etymology: Formed in Old French (renvoier, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + envoyer ('to send on one's way', from en + voie 'way' < Latin via).

history.meaning: to send back, return, dismiss/fire, refer, reflect

repartir.etymology: Formed in Old French (repartir, 12th c.) from iterative prefix re- ('again, back') + partir ('to set out, leave').

history.meaning: to set off again, leave again, start up again

repasser.etymology: Formed in Old French (repasser, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, back') + passer ('to pass'); developed the specialized senses of passing a blade over a whetstone ('to sharpen'), passing a hot iron over linen ('to iron clothes'), and going over a lesson again.

history.meaning: to pass by again; to whet a blade; to iron clothes

repeindre.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from iterative prefix re- ('again, anew') + peindre ('to paint').

history.meaning: to paint again, give a fresh coat of paint to

replier.etymology: Formed in Old French (repleier / replier, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + plier ('to fold, bend').

history.meaning: to fold back, fold up again, tuck in; (reflexive) to fall back, withdraw

reposer.etymology: Inherited from Old French reposer ('to rest, take rest, set down again'), from Late Latin repausare ('to cause to rest, pause'), compound of re- + pausare ('to pause, cease', from pausa 'a halt, pause' < Greek pausis).

history.meaning: to rest, lie at rest; to put back down

reprendre.etymology: Formed in Old French (reprendre, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + prendre ('to take', from Latin prehendere).

history.meaning: to take back, resume, have a second helping, alter a garment, reprove

représentante.etymology: Feminine form of représentant ('representative, agent, commercial traveler'), substantivized present participle of représenter ('to make present again, depict, act on behalf of', from Latin repraesentare).

history.meaning: female representative, delegate, or sales agent

respecter.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin respectare ('to look back at repeatedly, regard with deference or consideration'), frequentative of respicere, respectum ('to look back at, have regard for', from re- + specere 'to look').

history.meaning: to look back upon, show regard for
to treat with deference, respect, abide by (a rule)

respirer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin respirare ('to breathe out, fetch one's breath, breathe, recover breath'), compound of re- ('back and forth, again') + spirare ('to blow, breathe').

history.meaning: to breathe, take a breather, exude

responsable.etymology: Formed in the 13th–14th century in legal French from Medieval Latin responsabilis ('answerable in court'), derived from the supine stem respons- of Classical Latin respondere ('to answer, promise in return, be answerable for').

ressembler.etymology: Inherited from Old French resembler ('to be like, look like'), formed from prefix re- + sembler ('to seem, be alike', from Classical Latin similare 'to make like, resemble', from similis 'similar').

history.meaning: to bear a likeness to, resemble

resserrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (resserrer, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, more tightly') + serrer ('to press close, tighten, lock').

history.meaning: to tighten again, draw closer together, narrow

restaurer.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin restaurare ('to rebuild, renew, repair, restore'), from re- ('again') + *-staurare (built on the PIE root *sta- 'to stand', as in instaurare); in 18th-century Paris, un bouillon qui restaure ('a restorative broth') gave rise to restaurant.

history.meaning: to repair a building or artwork; to refresh with food and drink

rester.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin restare ('to stand back, stay behind, remain, be left over'), compound of re- ('back, behind') + stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: to remain, stay, be left over

retard.etymology: Retard is a noun formed from retarder, to delay. The Académie dates the noun to the seventeenth century. The modern expression en retard means late.

retenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French retenir ('to hold back, keep, detain, remember'), from Vulgar Latin *retenire for Classical Latin retinere ('to hold back, keep, preserve'), compound of re- ('back') + tenere ('to hold').

history.meaning: to hold back, detain, keep in memory, book/reserve, carry a digit

retour.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (retor / retour, 11th–12th c.) from retorner / retourner ('to turn back, return').

history.meaning: act of coming or going back, return, recurrence

retourner.etymology: Formed in Old French (retorner, 10th–11th c.) from prefix re- ('back, in the opposite direction') + torner / tourner ('to turn', from Classical Latin tornare 'to turn on a lathe').

history.meaning: to turn over, turn inside out, go back, return

retraite.etymology: Inherited from Old French retraite ('act of drawing back, military withdrawal, place of refuge'), substantivized feminine past participle of retraire ('to draw back, withdraw', from Classical Latin retrahere 'to draw back'); acquired the modern sense 'retirement from working life and old-age pension' in the 17th–19th centuries.

history.meaning: drawing back, military retreat, quiet refuge
military retreat, spiritual retreat; retirement and pension

retrouvailles.etymology: Formed in the 19th–20th century as a feminine plural noun from retrouver ('to find again, meet again after a separation') + festive/collective suffix -ailles (on the model of épousailles, fiançailles).

history.meaning: joyful reunion after a long separation

retrouver.etymology: Formed in Old French (retrover, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- ('again') + trover / trouver ('to find').

history.meaning: to find again, recover, meet up with, recognize

revenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French revenir ('to come back'), from Classical Latin revenire ('to come back, return'), compound of re- ('back, again') + venire ('to come').

history.meaning: to come back, return, recover consciousness, cost, brown lightly in pan

revisser.etymology: Formed in Modern French from iterative prefix re- ('again, back') + visser ('to screw in, fasten with screws', from vis 'screw').

history.meaning: to screw back on or tighten a screw again

revoir.etymology: Revoir is derived from voir, to see, with the idea of seeing again. The Académie records tenth-century revedeir and twelfth-century reveoir.

rez-de-chaussée.etymology: Compound noun formed in the 16th–17th century from archaic preposition rez ('flush with, at the exact level of', from Old French res < Classical Latin rasus 'scraped flat, level', past participle of radere) + de ('of') + chaussée ('paved street, roadway') — literally 'at street level'.

history.meaning: level with the street -> ground floor of a building

riche.etymology: Inherited from Old French riche ('powerful, mighty, noble; wealthy'), borrowed from Frankish *riki ('powerful, mighty, royal', from Proto-Germanic *rikijaz, cognate with English rich and German reich, itself an ancient Germanic borrowing from Celtic *rix 'king').

rideau.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (ridel / rideau, 13th–14th c., 'pleated cloth hanging around a bed or window') from rider ('to wrinkle, gather into pleats', from Frankish *hridan 'to twist, pleat, wrinkle').

history.meaning: pleated bed or window hanging -> curtain, stage curtain

rien.etymology: Rien descends from Latin rem, the object-case form of res, thing. The French word is recorded from the tenth century; negative constructions gave this older thing-word its familiar modern meaning nothing.

rime.etymology: Inherited from Old French rime ('accentual verse, correspondence of terminal sounds in poetry'), derived via Medieval Latin rithmus from Ancient Greek rhythmos ('measured flow, cadence, proportion'); in medieval Latin poetry, rhythmus designated accentual rhymed verse as opposed to classical quantitative meter (metrum).

rire.etymology: Inherited from Old French rire ('to laugh'), from Vulgar Latin *ridere, 3rd-conjugation shift of Classical Latin ridere ('to laugh, smile').

robe.etymology: Inherited from Old French robe (originally 'booty, spoils stripped from a fallen enemy, pillaged garments', then 'suit of outer clothing, gown'), borrowed from Frankish *rauba ('spoils of war, plunder, captured clothing', from Proto-Germanic *raubo, cognate with English rob and reave).

history.meaning: garment, judicial/academic gown, woman's dress, animal's coat, color of wine

robinet.etymology: Appeared in the 15th century as a nickname from Robin (pet form of the given name Robert, also used in medieval folklore as the name of the sheep in the Roman de Renart) because water spigots on casks and fountains were commonly cast with a decorative ram's head whose knob was turned to let water or wine flow.

history.form: Robin (name given to the ram) -> robinet
history.meaning: ram's-head cask spigot -> water tap, faucet, valve

rond.etymology: Inherited from Old French reont / roont ('round, circular'), from Classical Latin rotundus ('wheel-shaped, circular, spherical, well-rounded'), derived from rota ('wheel').

ronronner.etymology: Nineteenth-century French verb built on the reduplicated onomatopoeia ronron ('a cat's purr'), imitating a steady low vibration.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ronronner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ronronner

rose.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (rose, 11th–12th c.) from Classical Latin rosa ('rose flower and bush', an ancient Mediterranean word parallel to Greek rhodon); used as an adjective and noun for the color pink since the Middle Ages.

history.meaning: rose flower (fem. noun); pink color (adj. & masc. noun)

roue.etymology: Inherited from Old French roe ('wheel'), from Classical Latin rota ('wheel of a chariot or potter, disk', from PIE *roteh2 'wheel', built on *ret- 'to run, roll').

rouge.etymology: Inherited from Old French roge / rouge ('red'), from Classical Latin rubeus ('red, reddish', originally applied to cattle and hides, derived from ruber 'red' < PIE *h1rewdh- 'red'), which displaced ruber in Gallo-Romance.

rouleau.etymology: Inherited from Old French rolel / rouleau ('rolled-up scroll, cylinder'), diminutive of rôle (in its original sense 'parchment roll'), from Vulgar Latin *rotularius / Classical Latin rotulus ('little wheel, scroll'), diminutive of rota ('wheel').

history.meaning: scroll, cylindrical roller, rolling pin, paint roller, breaking wave

roulé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of rouler ('to roll, roll up'), designating a rolled pastry (biscuit roulé, Swiss roll) or rolled roast.

rouvrir.etymology: Formed in Old French (rovreir / rouvrir, 12th c.) from iterative prefix r- / re- ('again') + ouvrir ('to open').

ruban.etymology: Attested in thirteenth-century Old French as riban / ruban, likely borrowed from Middle Dutch ringhband ('neckband, collar ribbon'). Middle English riban—modern English ribbon—came straight from the Old Northern French form.

cognates.meaning: narrow woven strip (from Old French riban)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ruban (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ruban

rue.etymology: Rue comes from Late Latin ruga ('wrinkle, furrow', and by extension a 'wheel-rutted path' or 'lined street between houses'), developing into Old French rue ('town street').
rue.notes: Diminutive **une ruelle** = a narrow alley or side lane.

ruelle.etymology: Formed in Old French (ruele, 12th c.) as a diminutive of rue ('street', from Late Latin ruga 'wrinkle, furrow; wheel-rut, street lined with houses') + diminutive suffix -elle.

history.meaning: narrow lane or alley; space beside a four-poster bed

rythme.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century via Classical Latin rhythmus from Ancient Greek rhythmos ('measured motion, regular recurrence, cadence, proportion', related to rhein 'to flow' — learned doublet of rime).

history.meaning: musical, poetic, or biological rhythm, pace

règle.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned adaptation in Old French (reule / riule -> règle) from Classical Latin regula ('straight wooden lath, ruler, measuring rod; moral or monastic standard, rule'), derived from regere ('to keep straight, guide, rule').

règlement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from régler ('to rule lines, regulate, settle an account') + nominal suffix -ment.

history.meaning: body of regulations, bylaws; settlement or payment of a bill or dispute

ré.etymology: Second syllable of the hexachord introduced by Guido d'Arezzo (c. 1025), taken from the initial syllable of the second half-line (Resonare fibris) of the Latin hymn to St. John the Baptist Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: second solfège note of the scale (D)

réaliser.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century (originally in law and philosophy, 'to make real or actual, convert property into cash') from Medieval Scholastic Latin realis ('actual, relating to things', from Classical Latin res 'thing'); acquired the additional sense 'to become fully aware of, realize' in the late 19th century under the influence of English to realize.

history.meaning: to make real, carry out, direct a film; to realize mentally

réalité.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Medieval Scholastic Latin realitatem (nominative realitas, coined by Duns Scotus for 'actual existence as a thing'), derived from Late Latin realis ('relating to actual things'), from Classical Latin res ('thing, fact').

réception.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin receptionem (nominative receptio, 'a taking in, receiving, sheltering'), derived from recipere, receptum ('to receive').

history.meaning: receipt of goods/signals, formal social reception, hotel front desk

réceptionniste.etymology: Formed in the 20th century (modeled on English receptionist) from réception ('hotel or office reception desk') + specialist suffix -iste.

réduction.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin reductionem (nominative reductio, 'a leading or bringing back, restoration'), derived from reducere, reductum ('to lead back, bring to a smaller state'); developed the senses of scaling down a drawing, boiling down a sauce, and granting a price discount.

history.meaning: decrease, price discount, scaled-down copy, thickened culinary sauce

région.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin regionem (nominative regio, 'direction, boundary line, district, province, quarter of the sky or earth'), derived from regere ('to direct in a straight line, rule').

history.meaning: geographical or administrative region, body area

régler.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old/Middle French from Late Latin regulare ('to direct by a rule, regulate'), derived from Classical Latin regula ('straightedge ruler, rule'); combines the senses 'to draw straight lines with a ruler', 'to adjust a clock or machine', and 'to settle a bill or problem'.

history.meaning: to rule paper, adjust/set a mechanism, settle an account

régulier.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–13th century (originally in Church usage for clergy bound by a monastic rule, règle, as opposed to secular clergy) from Classical Latin regularis ('relating to a bar or rule'), derived from regula ('straightedge, rule').

history.meaning: bound by a rule -> uniform, steady, punctual, regular

réouverture.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from iterative prefix ré- ('again') + ouverture ('opening').

réparation.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Late Latin reparationem (nominative reparatio, 'restoration, renewal'), derived from Classical Latin reparare ('to restore, repair').

history.meaning: mending, repair; amends or compensation for damage

réparer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin reparare ('to get again, recover, renew, restore, put back in good order'), compound of re- ('again') + parare ('to prepare, make ready').

history.meaning: to make ready again, restore, mend
to repair, mend, fix, make amends for

répondre.etymology: Inherited from Old French respondre ('to answer, reply, correspond, stand surety for'), from Vulgar Latin *respondere, 3rd-conjugation shift of Classical Latin respondere ('to promise in return, answer, reply', from re- 'in return' + spondere 'to pledge solemnly').

history.meaning: to answer, reply, meet expectations, vouch for

réponse.etymology: Inherited from Old French response ('answer, reply'), from Vulgar Latin *responsa, feminine singular reshaped from Classical Latin neuter plural responsa ('answers, especially of jurists or oracles'), past participle of respondere ('to answer').

répéter.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin repetere ('to strike at again, return to, begin anew, say or do over again'), compound of re- ('again') + petere ('to seek, aim at').

history.meaning: to seek again, say or do over again
to repeat; to rehearse a play or concert

réservation.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (originally in canon law for the papal reservation of benefices) from Medieval Latin reservationem, derived from Classical Latin reservare ('to keep back, save up'); acquired the modern travel/hospitality sense ('advance booking of a seat, room, or table') in the 19th–20th century (reinforced by English reservation).

history.meaning: advance booking of a room, table, or ticket

réserve.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 14th–15th century from réserver ('to keep back for a later time, save', from Classical Latin reservare < re- 'back' + servare 'to keep, preserve').

history.meaning: stock kept back for future need, nature reserve, storeroom, cautious restraint

réserver.etymology: Réserver was borrowed from Latin reservare, to put aside or keep. The Académie records the French verb from the twelfth century.

résonner.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–15th century (reshaping Old French resoner) from Classical Latin resonare ('to sound again, echo back, resound'), compound of re- ('back, again') + sonare ('to sound', from sonus 'sound').

réunion.etymology: Réunion is derived from réunir. Its fifteenth-century senses included reconciliation or agreement before the broader idea of bringing together and the modern meeting sense.

réunir.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from iterative prefix ré- ('again, together') + unir ('to unite, join as one', from Late Latin unire < Classical Latin unus 'one').

history.meaning: to join together again, gather, bring together, convene a meeting

réveil.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (resveil, 12th–13th c., 'act of waking from sleep') from resveillier / réveiller ('to awaken', from re- + esveillier < Vulgar Latin *exvigilare 'to wake up'); also used by ellipsis for réveille-matin ('alarm clock').

réveiller.etymology: Réveiller is derived from éveiller, to wake. The Académie records the derivative from the twelfth century. The reflexive se réveiller describes waking up oneself.

réverbère.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 15th–18th century from réverbérer ('to reflect back light or heat', from Late Latin reverberare 'to beat back, reflect'); in 1745–1766, oil streetlamps fitted with concave polished metal reflectors (lanternes à réverbère) were installed across Paris, making réverbère the standard French word for a streetlamp.

history.meaning: reflecting mirror on an oil lamp -> streetlamp, lamppost

rêve.etymology: Rêve is a noun formed from rêver. The Académie records the noun from the seventeenth century; this account does not claim a settled deeper origin for rêver.

rêver.etymology: Inherited from Old French resver (12th c., originally 'to wander about deliriously, rave, talk wildly'), of debated origin (possibly from Vulgar Latin *re-ex-vadere 'to wander off track' or an expressive root); in the 16th–17th century it gradually took over the sense 'to dream while sleeping or daydreaming', displacing Old French songier (< somniare).

history.meaning: to wander about, rave in delirium

rôtir.etymology: Inherited from Old French rostir ('to roast meat on a spit or gridiron over an open fire'), borrowed from Frankish *raustjan ('to roast on a gridiron', from *raust 'gridiron', cognate with Old High German rosten and English roast).

history.meaning: to broil on a grate, roast over fire

s'arrêter.etymology: Pronominal form of arrêter ('to stop, bring to a halt'), from Old French s'arester (< Vulgar Latin *arrestare, from ad- + restare 'to stand still, remain').

history.meaning: to come to a halt, stop oneself
to stop, pause, cease doing something

s'asseoir.etymology: Asseoir descends from Vulgar Latin *assedere (Classical Latin assidere, ad + sedere 'to sit beside'). Reflexive **s'asseoir** means 'to sit down'.

s'endormir.etymology: Pronominal form of endormir ('to put to sleep'), formed in Old French (soi endormir, 11th–12th c.) from inchoative/intensive prefix en- (Latin in-) + dormir ('to sleep', from Classical Latin dormire).

s'envoler.etymology: Pronominal verb formed in Old French (soi en voler -> s'envoler) from adverbial pronoun en ('away from here', from Latin inde 'thence') + voler ('to fly', from Classical Latin volare).

history.meaning: to fly away, take wing, take off (of an aircraft), vanish

s'occuper.etymology: Pronominal form of occuper ('to take possession of, employ, busy'), from Classical Latin occupare; with de, means 'to take care of, attend to, look after'.

history.meaning: to keep oneself busy; to take care of, handle

sable.etymology: Inherited from Old French sable (alongside sablon, 'sand, gravel'), from Classical Latin sabulum ('coarse sand, gravel', which displaced arena in northern Gaul).

sac.etymology: Sac comes from Latin saccus ('bag, sack'), borrowed via Ancient Greek sákkos from Semitic *śaq ('coarse cloth, sack').
sac.notes: **Sac à main** = handbag; **sac à dos** = backpack.

sage.etymology: Inherited from Old French sage ('wise, learned, prudent'), from Vulgar Latin *sabius, contracted from Classical/Late Latin sapidus ('having taste or flavor; discerning, wise', derived from sapere 'to taste, have good discernment, be wise').

history.meaning: wise, sensible, well-behaved (of a child); wise person, sage (noun)

salle.etymology: Salle came through Latin sala from reconstructed Old Low Franconian *sal, a dwelling consisting of a single room. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

salon.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian salone ('great reception hall in a palace'), augmentative of sala ('hall, room', borrowed from Lombardic/Frankish *sala 'single-room dwelling, hall', source of French salle).

history.meaning: reception room, living room, literary gathering, trade exhibition, hair salon

saluer.etymology: Inherited from Old French saluer ('to wish health and safety to, greet, bow to'), from Classical Latin salutare ('to wish health to, greet, pay one's respects'), derived from salus, salutis ('health, safety, welfare, greeting').

history.meaning: to wish good health to, greet
to greet, say hello to, salute, hail

salut.etymology: Salut descends from Latin salus, physical well-being or health, related to salvus, safe or well. Wishing someone good health helped the word develop its greeting sense.

salé.etymology: Inherited from Old French salé ('salted, salty'), past participle of saler ('to salt, cure with salt'), from Classical Latin salare / *salire, derived from sal ('salt').

history.meaning: salty, savory (as opposed to sweet); steep (of a bill)

samedi.etymology: Inherited from Old French samedy / sambedi ('Saturday'), from Vulgar Latin *sambati dies (attested across Gaul, northern Italy, and the Balkans, reflecting a nasalized vernacular Greek pronunciation *sambaton), from Ecclesiastical Latin sabbati dies ('day of the Sabbath'), from Ancient Greek sabbaton < Hebrew shabbat ('rest, Sabbath').

sans.etymology: Inherited from Old French senz / sans ('without'), from Vulgar Latin *senis / Classical Latin sine ('without', reinforced in Gallo-Romance with adverbial -s, possibly blended with absentia in legal formulas).

sauf.etymology: Inherited from Old French salf / sauf ('unharmed, safe; save, except'), from Classical Latin salvus ('whole, uninjured, safe and sound'); the prepositional sense ('except, save for') arose from Latin ablative absolute constructions like salvo jure / salvo honore ('with one's right/honor kept intact, saving...').

history.meaning: safe and sound; keeping intact, excepting
safe and sound (sain et sauf, adj.); except, save for (prep.)

sauter.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin saltare ('to dance, leap, jump about'), frequentative of salire ('to leap, spring, bound').

history.meaning: to leap -> to jump repeatedly, dance

sauver.etymology: Sauver comes from Late Latin salvare ('to save, preserve', built on Classical Latin salvus 'safe, unharmed'). Vocalisation of l before v turned salvare into Old French salver, sauver.
sauver.notes: Related to **sauf** ('safe' in *sain et sauf*, and preposition 'except').

savoir.etymology: Savoir continues Latin sapere. That verb could refer both to taste or smell and to discernment or wisdom. The Académie dates French savoir to the ninth century: the history connects sensory judgement with knowing.
savoir.notes:
- *Savoir* is for facts and learned skills; *connaître* is for people, places and being familiar with something.
- *Je ne sais pas* is often shortened in speech to *chais pas*.

savon.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin saponem (nominative sapo, 'hair dye or tallow-and-ash mixture used by Gauls and Germans'), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *saipōn ('dripping resin, soap').

savonneux.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from savon ('soap', from Late Latin saponem) with the adjectival suffix -eux (from Latin -osus, 'full of, having the nature of').

savourer.etymology: Derived in the 12th century from Old French savour ('taste, flavor, relish', modern saveur, from Classical Latin saporem, from sapere 'to taste, have flavor').

sceau.etymology: Inherited via Old French seel ('signet ring, stamped wax emblem') from Classical Latin sigillum ('little figure, seal impression'), diminutive of signum ('mark, sign'); spelled sceau with etymological sc- from the Renaissance.

cognates.meaning: seal was borrowed from Old French seel!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: sceau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: sceau

sceau.notes: Famous French homophone quartet **/so/**: **un sceau** ('a wax seal'), **un seau** ('a bucket'), **un saut** ('a jump'), and **sot** ('foolish')!

sceller.etymology: Derived from Old French seel ('seal, signet', modern sceau, inherited from Classical Latin sigillum 'small figure, seal impression', diminutive of signum 'mark, sign').

history.meaning: to affix a seal, seal shut

sculpter.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally sculper, then reshaped after sculpteur / sculpture) from Classical Latin sculpere, past participle sculptus ('to carve,grave, chisel in stone, wood, or metal').

se.etymology: Se continues Latin se, oneself. It is recorded in French from the ninth century. Its modern reflexive uses belong to that pronoun history, not to the chemical abbreviation Se.

se souvenir.etymology: Pronominal construction of souvenir ('to come to mind, remember'), inherited from Classical Latin subvenire ('to come up from under, come to aid, occur to the mind'), from sub- ('under, up from below') + venire ('to come').

history.meaning: it comes to mind -> to remember

seau.etymology: Inherited via Old French seel from Vulgar Latin *sitellum, masculine diminutive of Classical Latin situla ('well bucket, pail').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: seau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: seau

seau.notes: Famous French homophone trio all pronounced `/so/`: **un seau** ('a bucket'), **un sceau** ('a wax seal', < *sigillum*), and **un saut** ('a jump', < *saltum*).

sec.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin siccus ('dry, parched, without moisture; sober').

seconde.etymology: From Medieval Latin (pars) minuta secunda ('second small division [of an hour or degree]'), feminine of Classical Latin secundus ('following, second in rank or order', from sequi 'to follow').

history.meaning: second (of time or arc); second class/gear

secret.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin secretus ('set apart, hidden, private') and its neuter noun secretum ('hidden thing, mystery, secluded place'), past participle of secernere ('to separate, set apart'), from se- ('apart') + cernere ('to sift, distinguish').

history.meaning: to separate -> set apart, hidden thing

seize.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sedecim ('sixteen'), compound of sex ('six') + decem ('ten').

sel.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin sal ('salt'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ls, one of the oldest and best-preserved culinary words across European languages.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: sel (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: sel

sel.notes: Latin *sal* also gave French **la salade** ('salted greens'), **la sauce** (*salsa* 'salted dressing'), and **le salaire** (*salarium*).

semaine.etymology: Semaine descends from Christian Latin septimana, related to an adjective meaning concerning the number seven. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

sembler.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin similare ('to resemble, be like, imitate'), derived from similis ('like, similar').

sens.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin sensus ('faculty of perceiving, feeling, understanding, meaning, direction'), from sentire ('to feel, perceive'), Later reinforced in directional meanings by Frankish *sinn ('direction, way').

sentimental.etymology: Borrowed in 1769 from English sentimental (popularized by Laurence Sterne's A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy, 1768), formed on sentiment ('feeling', itself from French sentiment) + -al.

history.meaning: characterized by tender emotion or feeling

sentir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sentire ('to perceive by the senses, feel, hear, smell, think').

history.meaning: to perceive by the senses, feel

sept.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin septem ('seven'), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ ('seven'). The silent p was reintroduced in Middle French orthography by learned Latinizing spelling.

serrure.etymology: Derived in the 12th century from serrer ('to bar, lock up, fasten tightly', from Late Latin serare 'to bolt, bar', from sera 'door-bar') + instrumental noun suffix -ure.

serré.etymology: Past participle of serrer ('to press close, tighten, lock'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *serrare, alteration of Late Latin serare ('to bolt, fasten shut', from Classical Latin sera 'crossbar, bolt') blended with serrare ('to saw').

service.etymology: Borrowed in the 11th century from Classical Latin servitium ('condition of a slave, servitude; body of servants'), derived from servus ('slave, servant'), broadened in medieval feudal and courtly usage to 'duty rendered, helpful act, table service'.

serviette.etymology: Serviette was formed in Middle French from servir ('to serve at table', from Latin servire) + diminutive -ette: originally the cloth used when serving at table, and later also a bath towel or briefcase.
serviette.notes: Context tells you whether **une serviette** is a napkin at breakfast or a towel in a hotel bathroom.

servir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin servire ('to be a slave or servant, be subject to, serve, be useful to'), derived from servus ('slave, servant').

history.meaning: servant -> to serve, be of use

seul.etymology: Seul continues Latin solus, alone or only. The Académie records the French adjective from the tenth century.

seulement.etymology: Formed in the 12th century from the feminine adjective seule ('alone, single, only', from Classical Latin solus) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

si.etymology: The conditional si continues Latin si, if. The affirmative reply si has a different source, Latin sic, thus or yes. The musical note with the same spelling has a separate history.

signaler.etymology: Derived in the 16th–17th century from signal ('visual or acoustic sign', from Medieval Latin signale, neuter of signalis, from signum 'mark, sign') or borrowed via Italian segnalare ('to mark out, distinguish').

signature.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Medieval Latin signatura ('matrix of a seal, official mark, handwritten name'), derived from Late Latin signare ('to mark, stamp, sign', from Classical Latin signum).

history.meaning: to seal, sign -> seal mark, signature

signe.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned inheritance from Classical Latin signum ('identifying mark, token, signal, military standard, constellation').

signer.etymology: Signer was remodelled after signe from older French seigner, which came from Latin signare, to mark or seal. The Académie distinguishes the thirteenth-century sense make a sign from the sixteenth-century signature sense.

silence.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin silentium ('state of being noiseless or still, silence'), derived from silens (present participle of silere 'to be noiseless, keep quiet').

simple.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin simplex, accusative simplicem ('single, uncompounded, plain, straightforward, guileless'), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- ('one') + *-plek- ('fold', cf. plicare 'to fold').

simplement.etymology: Formed in the 12th century from the adjective simple ('plain, straightforward', from Classical Latin simplex) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente).

sincère.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin sincerus ('clean, pure, sound, unspoiled, genuine, candid'), traditionally connected since antiquity with sine ('without') + cera ('wax', i.e. marble or honey free of wax), though modern Indo-Europeanists prefer *sm̥-kēros ('of one growth, whole, unmixed').

sinon.etymology: Formed in Old French (se non, si non) from the conditional conjunction si ('if', from Latin si) + the negation non ('not', from Latin non), modeling Classical Latin sinon / si non ('if not, otherwise').

six.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sex ('six'), from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs ('six').

siège.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from Old French asegier / segier ('to seat, settle, besiege'), from Popular Latin *sedicare, derived from Classical Latin sedere ('to sit', cf. sedes 'seat').

soi.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin se (stressed accusative and ablative reflexive pronoun 'oneself, himself, herself, themselves'), from Proto-Indo-European *swé ('oneself').

soie.etymology: Inherited via Old French seie / soie from Classical Latin saeta ('coarse animal hair, bristle'), which in Late Latin phrases like seta serica ('Seric/Chinese strand') shifted to mean 'silk thread, silk fabric'.

cognates.meaning: borrowed via French from Arabic zaytūnī

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: soie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: soie

soie.notes: Notice **le papier de soie**: in French, crisp ultra-thin wrapping tissue paper is poetically called 'silk paper'.

soigné.etymology: Past participle of soigner ('to take care of, attend to carefully'), derived from Old French soin ('care, attention, concern', from Frankish *sunnja 'legal excuse, care, solicitude').

history.meaning: care -> to tend carefully -> neat, well-groomed, carefully done

soir.etymology: Soir descends from Latin serus, late or of the evening. The Académie records tenth-century ser before the twelfth-century form soir.

soirée.etymology: Soirée is derived from soir. It is recorded from the thirteenth century and can refer to the evening as a period spent doing something, or to an evening event.

sol.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin solum ('bottom, ground, floor, soil, foundation').

soleil.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *soliculum (originally diminutive 'little sun', replacing short Classical Latin sol in Gallo-Romance), from Classical Latin sol ('sun') + diminutive suffix -iculus.

solide.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin solidus ('dense, compact, whole, firm, substantial'), related to salvus ('whole, safe') and solus ('whole').
