sombre.etymology: Post-verbal adjective formed in the 14th century from Old French sombrer ('to shade, be in shadow'), from Vulgar Latin *subumbrare ('to put under shade'), from Classical Latin sub- ('under') + umbra ('shadow, shade').

history.meaning: under shadow -> to cast into shade

son.etymology: The possessive son, with feminine sa, continues Latin suus, sua and suum. The Académie dates it to the ninth century. It is historically separate from the nouns son meaning sound or bran.

sonner.etymology: Sonner comes from Latin sonare ('to sound, ring, resound', from sonus 'sound'). It covers both ringing a bell and a clock striking the hour.
sonner.notes: Gives **la sonnette** ('bell, buzzer') and **la sonnerie** ('ringtone, chime').

sonnerie.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from sonner ('to ring, sound', from Classical Latin sonare, from sonus 'sound') + the collective/action noun suffix -erie.

sonnette.etymology: Derived in the 13th–14th century as a diminutive in -ette of Old French sonne ('little bell'), post-verbal noun from sonner ('to ring, sound', from Classical Latin sonare).

sortir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sortiri ('to draw lots, obtain by lot, divide'), which in Late and Gallo-Romance usage shifted via 'to obtain one's share and depart' (or blended with *surctus from surgere 'to rise') to 'to go out, come out, exit'.

history.meaning: to go out, exit, take out

souci.etymology: Souci derives from Old French soucier ('to trouble, worry', from Latin sollicitare 'to disturb, make anxious').
souci.notes: **Pas de souci!** = No worries! / No problem!

soucoupe.etymology: Formed from sous ('under') + coupe ('cup, goblet', or modelled on Italian sottocoppa). Originally a small footed salver held underneath a goblet when serving wine at table; with the arrival of tea, coffee, and chocolate in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, it became the modern saucer.

history.meaning: tray held beneath a drinking goblet
porcelain or earthenware saucer under a teacup

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: soucoupe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: soucoupe

souffle.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from souffler ('to blow, breathe'), inherited from Classical Latin sufflare ('to blow up from below, inflate, puff'), from sub- ('under, up') + flare ('to blow').

souffler.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sufflare ('to blow up from below, inflate, puff out'), compound of sub- ('under, up from beneath') + flare ('to blow').

souhaiter.etymology: Formed in the 12th century (Old French soushaidier) from sous- ('under', from Latin sub-) + Old French haitier ('to cheer, wish well, gladden'), derived from Frankish *hait ('promise, vow, command, wish').

history.meaning: to cheer, wish -> to desire, wish for

soulagement.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from soulager ('to lighten a burden, relieve, comfort') + -ment; soulager comes from Old French soulas ('relief, solace', from Classical Latin solacium) blended with léger ('light in weight', from Vulgar Latin *leviarius).

history.meaning: relief, easing of pain or worry

soulever.etymology: Soulever comes from Old French souzlever (sous 'under' + lever 'to raise', from Latin sublevare): literally 'to lift from underneath'.

soupe.etymology: Soupe comes from Late Latin suppa (of Germanic origin, related to English 'sop' and 'sup'), originally meaning the slice of bread placed in a bowl over which hot broth was poured, and later the soup itself.
soupe.notes: **Un bol de soupe chaude** = a bowl of hot soup.

souple.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin supplex, accusative supplicem ('bending the knees, humble, submissive, entreating'), from sub- ('under, down') + plac- / *plek- ('to fold, bend'); in French the physical sense 'bending easily, pliant, flexible' prevailed.

sourcil.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin supercilium ('eyebrow; ridge, pride'), compound of super- ('above, over') + cilium ('eyelid', whence French cil 'eyelash').

souriant.etymology: Present participle used as an adjective of sourire ('to smile'), inherited from Classical Latin subridere ('to smile slightly'), from sub- ('under, slightly') + ridere ('to laugh').

sourire.etymology: Substantivized infinitive of sourire ('to smile'), inherited from Classical Latin subridere (Vulgar Latin *subridere), compound of sub- ('under, slightly, quietly') + ridere ('to laugh').

souris.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *soricem (reshaped from Classical Latin sorex, accusative soricem 'shrew-mouse', from Greek hyrax), which displaced Classical Latin mus ('mouse') in Gallo-Romance.

sous.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin subtus ('below, underneath'), adverbial derivative of sub ('under').

souvenir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin subvenire ('to come up from beneath, come to mind, occur to someone'), from sub- ('under, up') + venire ('to come'); used both as a verb ('to remember') and as a substantivized infinitive ('memory, keepsake').

history.meaning: to come up, come to mind

souvent.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin subinde ('immediately after, repeatedly, from time to time'), compound of sub ('under, close upon') + inde ('thence, after that').

square.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from English square ('open landscaped urban square'), itself from Anglo-Norman esquire / Old French esqarre ('square', from Vulgar Latin *exquadrare, from Latin quadrus 'square').

history.meaning: small fenced public garden in a city

stable.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin stabilis ('standing firm, steadfast, enduring, unwavering'), derived from stare ('to stand') + instrument/ability suffix -bilis.

stand.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English stand ('raised platform or spectator grandstand at a racecourse; exhibition booth, shooting stall'), from the verb stand (Old English standan, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-).

history.meaning: exhibition booth, market stall, shooting range, pit stop

stop.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th–19th century (first in nautical, telegram, and traffic usage) from English stop ('halt! stop!'), from Old English *stoppian, ultimately from Late Latin stuppare ('to plug with tow').

history.meaning: to halt; halt command or traffic sign

stressé.etymology: Stressé is the past participle of stresser used as an adjective. Stresser is a twentieth-century derivative of stress; it is not an adjective whose origin can be inferred from the last letters alone.

strict.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin strictus ('drawn tight, close, exact, severe'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, compress'; doublet of inherited étroit).

history.meaning: to bind tight -> drawn tight, rigorous

stupéfait.etymology: Adapted in the 18th century (replacing earlier stupéfact) from Classical Latin stupefactus ('stunned, benumbed, astonished'), past participle of stupefacere ('to strike dumb, stun'), from stupere ('to be stunned or numb') + facere ('to make').

history.meaning: to be numb + to make -> stunned, astonished

style.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin stilus ('pointed writing instrument for wax tablets; manner of writing, mode of expression'), spelled with y under the false humanist association with Greek stylos ('pillar, column').

history.meaning: writing stylus -> manner of writing, literary style
style, manner of expression or design

stylo.etymology: Stylo is a twentieth-century shortening of stylographe. The shortened form became the ordinary French word for a pen.

stylo-plume.etymology: Twentieth-century compound of stylo (shortening of stylographe 'fountain pen', coined from Greek stylos 'pillar, writing rod' + -graphe) and plume ('feather, pen nib', from Classical Latin pluma 'downy feather').

sucre.etymology: Sucre entered Old French via Medieval Latin succarum and Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, which traced back through Persian šakar to Sanskrit śárkarā ('gravel, grit, crystal sugar').

sucré.etymology: Past participle of sucrer ('to sweeten with sugar'), derived from sucre ('sugar', borrowed via Medieval Latin succarum and Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, from Persian šakar and Sanskrit śarkarā 'gravel, candied sugar').

sud.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Old English sūþ ('south', via Anglo-Norman maritime usage), from Proto-Germanic *sunþaz ('south, toward the sun').

suffire.etymology: Inherited (with stem reshaping on faire) from Classical Latin sufficere ('to put under, supply, be enough, suffice'), compound of sub- ('under') + facere ('to make, do').

suite.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequita ('act of following, retinue, continuation'), substantivized feminine past participle of *sequire (Classical Latin sequi 'to follow').

suivant.etymology: Present participle of suivre ('to follow', from Vulgar Latin *sequire, Classical Latin sequi), used as an adjective ('following, next') and preposition ('according to').

suivre.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequere (regularized active infinitive of Classical Latin deponent sequi 'to follow, come after, pursue'), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- ('to follow').

history.meaning: to follow, attend, keep up with

sujet.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in the 12th century from Classical Latin subjectus / subiectus ('lying under, subjected; subject matter, underlying theme'), past participle of subicere ('to throw or place under'), from sub- ('under') + iacere ('to throw').

history.meaning: to place under -> subordinate, underlying topic
subject, topic, grammatical or political subject

super.etymology: Informal super is a twentieth-century use derived from the super- word family. The Académie distinguishes this favourable adjective or exclamation from the noun for a type of fuel.

sur.etymology: Sur continues Latin super, on or above. The French preposition is recorded from the ninth century. It is separate from the accented adjective sûr.

surtout.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the prepositional phrase sur tout ('above all, over everything'), from sur ('on, above', from Latin super) + tout ('all', from Latin totus / *tottus).

surveiller.etymology: Formed in the 16th–17th century from sur- ('over, above', from Latin super-) + veiller ('to stay awake, keep watch', from Classical Latin vigilare 'to be awake, watch').

survivre.etymology: Inherited or adapted in the 12th century from Late Latin supervivere ('to live beyond, outlive, survive'), compound of super- ('beyond, over') + vivere ('to live').

suspendre.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin suspendere ('to hang up, support from above, interrupt, keep in suspense'), from sub- ('under, up from beneath') + pendere ('to hang, weigh').

symbole.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Late Latin symbolum / symbolus ('token, creed, sign'), from Ancient Greek symbolon ('tally-piece, token of identity, sign'), from sym- ('together') + ballein ('to throw').

history.meaning: to throw together, match -> matching token, sign

sympa.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial apocope (clipping) of sympathique ('likeable, congenial, nice'), itself derived from sympathie (from Late Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek sympatheia 'fellow-feeling', from syn- 'with' + pathos 'feeling').

sécher.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin siccare ('to make dry, dry up, drain'), derived from the adjective siccus ('dry').

sécurité.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–15th century from Classical Latin securitas (accusative securitatem 'freedom from care, safety, security'), derived from securus ('free from care, safe', from se- 'without' + cura 'care, worry'; doublet of sûreté).

séjour.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 11th–12th century from Old French sojorner ('to stay for a time, rest, tarry', modern séjourner), from Vulgar Latin *subdiurnare ('to last for a day, stay awhile'), from sub- ('under, during') + diurnus ('of the day', from dies 'day').

history.meaning: to spend the day, abide for a while

sûr.etymology: Sûr descends from Latin securus, free from concern or safe. The Académie records it from the eleventh century. The written accent distinguishes it from the unrelated preposition sur.

sûrement.etymology: Formed in the 12th century from the feminine adjective sûre (Old French seüre, inherited from Classical Latin securus 'free from care, safe, certain') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

table.etymology: Table comes from Latin tabula ('board, plank, writing tablet, table'), passing through Old French table into both modern French and English.
table.notes: **À table!** = Dinner/breakfast is ready!; **tablette** ('shelf; digital tablet') is its diminutive.

tableau.etymology: Derived in the 12th–13th century (Old French tablel) as a diminutive in -el / -eau of table ('board, plank, writing or painting tablet', inherited from Classical Latin tabula 'board, plank, painted panel, list').

history.meaning: small board -> painted panel, picture, board, chart

tablette.etymology: Derived in the 12th–13th century as a diminutive in -ette of table ('board, plank, tablet', inherited from Classical Latin tabula 'board, flat slab, writing tablet').

history.meaning: small shelf, lozenge/bar (of chocolate), electronic tablet

tablier.etymology: Inherited from Old French tablier (originally 'tablecloth', 'board for table games', and by the 15th century 'protective cloth worn in front at a workbench or kitchen table'), derived from table (< Latin tabula 'board, table').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tablier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tablier

tablier.notes: In civil engineering, **le tablier d'un pont** still preserves the older 'flat planked board' sense: it means the deck of a bridge.

tabouret.etymology: Formed in Middle French as the diminutive of Old French tabour ('cylindrical drum', an older cousin of tambour), because early round low stools were shaped like small drums!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tabouret (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tabouret

tabouret.notes: At the court of Versailles, being granted **le tabouret**—the right to sit on a folding stool in the Queen's presence—was one of the highest honours in France.

tache.etymology: Inherited from Old French tache / teche ('mark, badge, natural trait, blemish, stain'), from Vulgar Latin *tacca ('mark, spot, clasp'), borrowed from a Gothic or West Germanic *taikn ('sign, token, mark', cf. English token, German Zeichen).

taille.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from tailler ('to cut, prune, shape, carve'), inherited from Late Latin taliare ('to split, cut, prune shoots'), derived from Classical Latin talea ('cutting, twig, slip for planting').

talon.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *talonem (augmentative in -o, -onis of Classical Latin talus 'ankle-bone, heel').

tampon.etymology: Nasalized variant of Middle French tapon ('cloth plug, bung, stopper'), borrowed from Frankish *tappo ('plug, tap, peg'); shifted from a pad of cloth dabbed in ink to an ink stamp or postmark.

history.meaning: plug, wadded pad -> inked stamping pad

cognates.meaning: cognate from Old English tæppa ('cask plug, faucet')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tampon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tampon

tampon.notes: On French mail and official notices, **le cachet / le tampon de la poste faisant foi** ('postmark serving as proof of date') is a classic administrative phrase.

tant.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tantum ('so much, to such a degree, only'), neuter adverbial accusative of tantus ('so great, so much').

history.meaning: so great -> so much, to such an extent
so much, so many, as much

tante.etymology: Alteration by nursery reduplication in the 13th century of Old French ante ('aunt'), inherited from Classical Latin amita ('father's sister, paternal aunt').

taper.etymology: Attested since the 12th century ('to strike with the flat of the hand, slap, tap, bung'), from a Gallo-Romance or Germanic expressive root *tapp- ('to strike, slap, plug with a bung', cf. Middle Dutch tappen).

history.meaning: expressive root: to slap, tap, stopper
to pat, hit, tap, type on a keyboard

tapis.etymology: Inherited from Old French tapiz, borrowed via Medieval Latin tapetium from Byzantine Greek tapētion (diminutive of Ancient Greek tapēs, stem tapēt- 'carpet, rug, tapestry').

tard.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tarde ('slowly, late'), adverb formed on tardus ('slow, sluggish, tardy, late').

tarte.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French tarte ('flat open pastry'), related to Medieval Latin tarta / torta ('round loaf or twisted pastry'). English tart was borrowed directly from Old French tarte.

cognates.meaning: open pastry pie (borrowed from Old French tarte)

rootFamily.gloss: buttered slice of bread with spread

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tarte (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tarte

tartine.etymology: Attested from the sixteenth century (Rabelais) as a playful diminutive (-ine) of tarte: a slice of bread spread open-faced with butter, jam, or honey like a little flat tart.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tartine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tartine

tasse.etymology: Tasse entered Old French (via Provençal tassa or Italian tazza) from Arabic ṭāsa ('shallow metal drinking bowl'), itself borrowed from Persian tāšt ('cup, basin').
tasse.notes: **Une tasse de thé / de café** = a cup of tea / coffee.

taxi.etymology: Early 20th-century clipping of taximètre ('fare-meter cab', altered from taxamètre, coined in Germany in 1890 as Taxameter from Medieval Latin taxa 'tax, fixed rate of fare' + Greek metron 'measure').

te.etymology: Te continues Latin te, the accusative form of tu, the second-person singular pronoun. The Académie records the French word from the tenth century. Modern te is the unstressed object form alongside subject tu and stressed toi; it is shortened to t' before a vowel or silent h.

tellement.etymology: Formed in the 12th–13th century from the feminine adjective telle ('such', inherited from Classical Latin talis 'of such a kind') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: in such a way -> so much, so

temporel.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin temporalis ('lasting for a time, belonging to time, secular/worldly'), derived from tempus, stem tempor- ('time, season').

temps.etymology: Temps continues Latin tempus, which referred to a division of duration, a season or time. The Académie also connects its weather sense with Latin caeli tempus, the state of the sky. That history helps explain why one French word covers both time and weather.

history.meaning: time, a division of duration, season
state of the sky; behind the weather sense

tendre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tendere ('to stretch, extend, direct, hold out, strive'), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- ('to stretch'). (Homonymous adjective tendre 'tender' comes from Latin tenerum.)

tenir.etymology: Tenir developed from Popular Latin tenire, a remodelling of Classical Latin tenere, to hold or keep. The Académie records the French verb from the tenth century.

tenter.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation in the 12th century from Classical Latin temptare / tentare ('to handle, test, try, attempt, assail'), frequentative of tendere ('to stretch') or tenere ('to hold').

terminer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin terminare ('to mark off by boundaries, limit, bring to an end, finish'), derived from terminus ('boundary stone, limit, end').

history.meaning: boundary, end -> to bound, bring to an end

terre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin terra ('dry land, earth, ground, soil, country'), from Proto-Indo-European *ters- ('dry', cf. Latin torrere 'to parch').

terrible.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin terribilis ('frightful, dreadful, inspiring terror'), derived from terrere ('to frighten, terrify').

test.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th–19th century (first in political/religious history, then in psychology and science) from English test ('trial, examination'), itself borrowed from Old French test ('earthenware pot or cupel used by alchemists to assay gold and silver', from Latin testum 'earthen vessel').

history.meaning: assay of metal -> critical trial, examination

tester.etymology: Derived in the late 19th–20th century from test ('examination, trial', borrowed from English test) or adapted directly from English to test. (Homonymous legal verb tester 'to make a will' comes from Latin testari.)

history.meaning: to subject to a test, try out

thym.etymology: Refashioned with learned Greek-Latin spelling from Old French tin, borrowed via Classical Latin thymum from Ancient Greek thýmon ('thyme'), connected to thýein ('to burn fragrant offerings, send up sweet smoke').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French tym, likewise given learned th- spelling

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: thym (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: thym

thym.notes: Tied with **persil** and bay leaf (**laurier**) using kitchen **ficelle**, **le thym** forms the classic French **bouquet garni**.

thé.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century via Dutch thee (and Malay teh) from Hokkien Chinese tê ('tea'), brought through maritime trade, whereas land-route varieties of Chinese cha gave Russian čaj and Portuguese chá.
thé.notes: Gives **la théière** ('teapot'). **Du thé au citron / à la menthe** = lemon / mint tea.

théière.etymology: Théière was coined in late seventeenth-century French from thé ('tea') + the vessel suffix -ière (modelled on cafetière 'coffee pot').

ticket.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from English ticket ('printed slip giving admission or receipt'), itself an early modern English borrowing of Middle French estiquet / étiquette ('small note or label pinned to a bag or door', from Old French estiquier 'to stick, attach', from Frankish *stikkan).

tige.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tibia ('shinbone, pipe, flute'), which shifted in Gallo-Romance to mean 'plant stalk, stem, shaft'.

tilleul.etymology: Tilleul comes from Popular Latin *tiliolus, diminutive of Classical Latin tilia ('linden or lime tree'), via Old French tilluel. Fragrant linden trees have shaded French courtyards and village squares for centuries.
tilleul.notes: In cafés, **un tilleul** also means a calming evening infusion made from dried linden blossoms.

tirer.etymology: Attested since the 11th century ('to pull, tug, tear, draw, shoot'); probable back-formation from Old French martirer ('to torture on the rack, tear apart', from Late Latin martyriare), or from a Romance root *tirare.

tiroir.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from tirer ('to pull, draw out') + the instrumental/locative suffix -oir (from Latin -orium), literally 'that which one pulls out'.

tisane.etymology: Inherited via Old French tisane from Classical Latin ptisana, borrowed from Ancient Greek ptisánē ('peeled barley, soothing warm barley-water infusion', from ptíssein 'to hull or crush grain'), which broadened from medicinal barley water to any gentle herbal infusion.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tisane (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tisane

tisane.notes: At the Hôtel du Tilleul, the tree in the courtyard itself provides one of France's favourite evening *tisanes*: **une tisane de tilleul** (linden-blossom tea).

tisser.etymology: Rebuilt in the 16th century (replacing irregular Old French tistre, from Classical Latin texere 'to weave, plait, construct') on the stem of the past participle tissu and derivatives like tisserand.

tissu.etymology: Substantivized past participle (Old French tissu 'woven', formed with suffix -u from Latin -utus) of Old French tistre ('to weave', from Classical Latin texere).

history.meaning: woven -> woven fabric, cloth, biological tissue

titre.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned inheritance in the 11th–12th century from Classical Latin titulus ('inscription, label, heading, title of honor, legal claim').

history.meaning: title, heading, legal right, financial security

tiède.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tepidus ('lukewarm, tepid, mildly warm'), derived from tepere ('to be moderately warm').

toi.etymology: Toi is the stressed pronoun descending from Latin te ('thee, you' accusative): in stressed position Latin long e diphthongised through ei and oi to modern /twa/.
toi.notes: Used after prepositions (*pour toi*, *avec toi*), in *c'est toi*, and in familiar imperatives (*Assieds-toi*).

toile.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tela ('woven web, cloth on the loom, warp'), from *texla, derived from texere ('to weave').

toilé.etymology: Derived in the 19th–20th century as a participial adjective from toile ('linen or canvas cloth', from Classical Latin tela), meaning 'bound in or having the texture of canvas/cloth'.

toit.etymology: Toit descends regularly from Latin tectum ('roof', originally the past participle of tegere 'to cover', cognate with English 'thatch'): -ct- gave -it and e + i evolved through oi to /wa/.
toit.notes: **Sous les toits** = up under the eaves (attic rooms).

tomate.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Spanish tomate, itself borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tomatl ('tomatillo, tomato', from tomohuac 'plump, fat, swollen').

tomber.etymology: Inherited from Old French tomber ('to do a somersault, tumble, fall'), from a Gallo-Romance expressive root *tumb- ('to fall with a thud, tumble') or Frankish *tumbōn ('to turn somersaults, dance, fall'), which gradually displaced Old French cheoir (from Latin cadere).

history.meaning: to tumble, somersault, fall with a thud

ton.etymology: The possessive ton, with feminine ta, continues Latin tuus, tua and tuum. It is recorded in French from the tenth century. The noun ton for tone has a different Greek and Latin history.

tonalité.etymology: Coined in 1810–1821 by musicologist Alexandre-Étienne Choron (and popularized by Fétis) from tonal ('relating to musical tone/key', from ton, from Latin tonus and Greek tonos 'tension, pitch') + abstract suffix -ité.

history.meaning: musical tonality, key, overall color/tone of voice

torchon.etymology: Inherited from Old French torchon ('twisted wisp of straw or coarse cloth used for wiping'), derived from torcher ('to wipe, rub clean') < Vulgar Latin *torquare, from Classical Latin torquere ('to twist').

history.meaning: to twist -> to twist straw into a scrubbing wisp

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French torche ('twisted resinous tow'), from the same root!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: torchon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: torchon

torchon.notes: Hence the classic French saying against mixing unlike things: **Il ne faut pas mélanger les torchons et les serviettes** ('Don't mix kitchen dishcloths with table napkins').

tordre.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torquere (3rd conjugation reshaping of Classical Latin torquere 'to twist, wind, wring, wrench, distort'), from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- ('to twist, turn').

torsion.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin torsionem (nominative torsio, Classical Latin tortio 'twisting, wringing, griping pain'), derived from torquere, past participle tortus / *torsus ('to twist').

tort.etymology: Inherited from Medieval/Vulgar Latin tortum ('injustice, wrong', substantivized neuter of Classical Latin tortus 'twisted, crooked, awry', past participle of torquere 'to twist'), contrasting with droit ('straight, right', from directum).

totalement.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from the feminine adjective totale ('entire, complete', borrowed from Medieval Latin totalis, from Classical Latin totus 'all, whole') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

touchant.etymology: Present participle of toucher ('to touch, strike, move emotionally'), used as a preposition ('concerning, regarding') since the 13th century and as an adjective ('moving, poignant') since the 16th–17th century.

touche.etymology: Deverbal noun from toucher ('to touch, strike lightly', from Spoken Latin *toccare, originally an expressive verb for knocking or striking a bell). By the sixteenth century une touche named each lever key touched by a player's fingers on an organ, harpsichord, and later piano.

history.meaning: to touch, strike -> act of touching

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: touche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: touche

toucher.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *toccare ('to knock, strike a bell, touch'), an expressive onomatopoeic formation (*tokk- 'knock, tap') attested across Romance (cf. Italian toccare, Spanish tocar).

toujours.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (toz jorz) of the plural phrase tous jours ('all days'), from tous (plural of tout 'all', from Latin totus / *tottus) + jours (plural of jour 'day', from Late Latin diurnum).

tour.etymology: Two homonyms merged in spelling: (1) masculine tour ('turn, circuit, lathe, trick'), post-verbal from tourner or inherited from Classical Latin tornus ('lathe', from Greek tornos); (2) feminine tour ('tower'), inherited from Classical Latin turris (accusative turrem 'tower').

tourner.etymology: Tourner descends from Latin tornare, to shape on a lathe, related to tornus, a lathe. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century and acquired many senses beyond physical turning.

tournevis.etymology: Transparent verb-noun compound attested from the late seventeenth century: tourne ('turns', from tourner) + vis ('screw', Old French vis 'winding stair, screw thread', from Latin vitis 'climbing vine tendril'). Literally 'screw-turner'.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tournevis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tournevis

tout.etymology: Tout continues Latin totus, all or whole. The Académie records it from the ninth century. The forms toute, tous and toutes belong to the same French word family.

trac.etymology: Nineteenth-century colloquial specialization ('sudden fright, stage fright') of Middle/Old French trac ('track of an animal, clatter, bustle'), from an expressive onomatopoeic root *trak- imitating a sharp noise or tread.

trace.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from tracer ('to follow a track, draw a line'), from Vulgar Latin *tractiare ('to drag, draw a line, track'), derived from Classical Latin tractus (past participle of trahere 'to pull, drag').

history.meaning: to draw along, leave a track

tracer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tractiare ('to drag, draw out, trace a path'), derived from Classical Latin tractus, past participle of trahere ('to draw, pull, drag').

history.meaning: to draw -> to draw a line, track
to trace, draw, lay out a route

train.etymology: Train is a noun built in Old French from traîner ('to drag, draw along', from Popular Latin *traginare). Before railways, un train meant a line of packhorses, carriages, or attendants; in the nineteenth century it naturally named a railway train.
train.notes: **Voyage en train** = train journey; **être en train de** = to be in the middle of doing.

trait.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tractus ('drawing, pulling, stroke of a pen, feature, stretch'), action noun from trahere ('to pull, draw, drag'; Old French traire).

history.meaning: to pull, draw -> pull, pen stroke, line
drawn missile/arrow, line, stroke, facial feature, gulp

tranche.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 13th century from tranchier / trancher ('to cut off, slice, sever'), probably from Vulgar Latin *trincare (alteration of Classical Latin truncare 'to lop off, maim, cut short', from truncus 'trunk, maimed').

tranquille.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin tranquillus ('calm, still, quiet, untroubled', originally of calm weather or sea), from trans- + a root related to quies ('rest, quiet').

transformation.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late/Christian Latin transformationem (nominative transformatio 'change of shape, metamorphosis'), action noun from Classical Latin transformare ('to change in shape, transform').

history.meaning: to change shape -> change of form

transformer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin transformare ('to change in shape, metamorphose, alter'), compound of trans- ('across, beyond') + formare ('to shape, form', from forma).

history.meaning: to shape across -> to change in form

travail.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from travailler ('to torment, labor painfully, work'), from Vulgar Latin *tripaliare ('to torture with the tripalium'), derived from Late Latin tripalium ('three-staked instrument of torture or restraint frame for shoeing horses', from tri- 'three' + palus 'stake').

travailler.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tripaliare ('to torture with a three-staked frame'), derived from Late Latin tripalium (attested in 582 CE at the Council of Auxerre, from tri- 'three' + palus 'stake'); evolved in Old French from 'to torment, suffer, labor in childbirth' to 'to toil, work'.

travers.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin transversus / Late Latin traversus ('turned across, lying crosswise, athwart'), past participle of transvertere ('to turn across'), from trans- ('across') + vertere ('to turn').

traverser.etymology: Inherited from Late/Vulgar Latin *traversare ('to cross over, place crosswise'), derived from Classical Latin transversus ('turned across, crosswise').

treillis.etymology: Derived in the 12th century (Old French treliz 'coarse triple-thread fabric; latticework, iron grate') from Vulgar Latin *trilicium, from Classical Latin trilix, accusative trilicem ('woven with three sets of leashes/threads', from tri- 'three' + licium 'heddle thread'), blended with treille ('vine arbor', from trichila).

trembler.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tremulare ('to shake, shiver, tremble'), derived from Classical Latin tremulus ('shaking, quivering', from tremere 'to tremble').

tremper.etymology: Inherited by metathesis of r from Classical Latin temperare ('to mix in due proportion, moderate, steep, temper red-hot iron by plunging it into water'), whence Old French temprer -> tremper ('to soak, dip, drench, temper steel').

history.meaning: to mix proportionally, steep, temper metal in liquid

trente.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trienta, contraction of Classical Latin triginta ('thirty'), from tres / tri- ('three') + -ginta ('tens').

trente-cinq.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from trente ('thirty', from Latin triginta) + cinq ('five', from Latin quinque / Vulgar Latin *cinque).

trente-huit.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from trente ('thirty', from Latin triginta) + huit ('eight', from Latin octo).

trentième.etymology: Derived in the 12th century from trente ('thirty', from Latin triginta) + the ordinal suffix -ième (Old French -isme, from Latin -esimus).

triste.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned inheritance in the 12th century from Classical Latin tristis ('sad, sorrowful, gloomy, bitter, harsh').

trois.etymology: Trois descends from Latin tres, three. The Académie dates the French form to the tenth century.

troisième.etymology: Formed in the 13th century from trois ('three', from Classical Latin tres) + the ordinal suffix -ième (replacing earlier inherited tiers, from Latin tertius, in general ordinal usage).

trop.etymology: Grammaticalized in Old French from the noun trop ('flock, herd, heap, large quantity', cf. troupe), borrowed from Frankish *þorp ('cluster of farms, village, crowd of people', cf. German Dorf, Old English þorp).

trottoir.etymology: Formed in French from trotter ('to trot, walk briskly', borrowed from Old High German troton) + place/instrument suffix -oir; first attested for a raised path for horses, then adopted in 1780s Paris for raised stone pedestrian walkways.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: trottoir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: trottoir

trottoir.notes: Paris built some of its first stone **trottoirs** along the Rue de l'Odéon in 1781 so pedestrians could step clear of muddy carriage wheels.

trou.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *traucum ('hole, perforation', attested in the 8th-century Lex Ripuaria as traugum), of Gaulish or pre-Latin substrate origin.

trouver.etymology: Trouver is traced to reconstructed Popular Latin *tropare, originally inventing rhetorical turns, tunes or verses. The meaning broadened through invent or discover to find. The French word is recorded from the tenth century.

très.etymology: Très developed from Latin trans, beyond, then through and completely. The Académie dates it to the eleventh century. Its modern intensifying sense continues that strengthening use.

trébucher.etymology: Inherited from Old French trebuchier ('to lose one's balance, stumble, topple, overturn'), formed from trans- / très- ('beyond, over') + Old French buc ('trunk of the body, torso', from Frankish *būk 'belly, trunk'), literally 'to pitch the body/trunk over'.

history.meaning: to topple body-first -> to stumble, trip

trésor.etymology: Inherited via Old French tresor (with early Gallo-Romance insertion of -r-) from Classical Latin thesaurus ('hoard, treasury'), borrowed from Ancient Greek thēsaurós ('storehouse, treasure chest').

cognates.meaning: treasure came from Old French tresor; thesaurus directly from Greco-Latin

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: trésor (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: trésor

trésor.notes: **Trésor** and English **thesaurus** ('a treasure-house of words') are exact doublets!

tu.etymology: Tu continues Latin tu, the second-person singular pronoun. The Académie dates the French word to the tenth century. Its familiar singular use today continues a very old grammatical distinction between addressing one person and addressing several.

tutoyer.etymology: Tutoyer was built in sixteenth-century French from the pronoun tu ('familiar you') + toi + -er, meaning 'to address someone using tu rather than vous'.
tutoyer.notes: Its polite counterpart is **vouvoyer** ('to address using *vous*'). **On se tutoie?** = Shall we use *tu*?

tuyau.etymology: Inherited from Old French tüel ('pipe, tube, nozzle, hollow stalk'), borrowed from Frankish *tūta ('hollow pipe, spout', cf. Middle Dutch tūte, German Tute / Düse) with the Romance suffix -el / -eau.

tâche.etymology: Inherited from Old French tasche / tasque ('fixed assessment, piecework job'), from Medieval Latin tasca ('tax, assessment, assigned work'), by metathesis from Late Latin taxa, post-verbal noun from Classical Latin taxare ('to touch sharply, appraise, value, rate').

history.meaning: to appraise, rate -> fixed assessment, assigned work

téléphone.etymology: Coined in the 19th century (first for acoustic signaling devices by Sudre in 1828, then applied in 1876 to Alexander Graham Bell's electric telephone) from Ancient Greek tēle- ('far off, at a distance') + phōnē ('voice, sound').

tête.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin testa ('earthenware pot, jug, tile, shell'), which came to be used in Late and Vulgar Latin slang (like English 'jug' or 'mug') for the 'skull' and 'head', displacing Classical Latin caput ('head', whence chef).

têtu.etymology: Derived in the 12th century (Old French testu 'having a big or hard head; stubborn') from teste ('head', modern tête, from Latin testa) + the adjectival suffix -u (from Latin -utus).

un.etymology: Un descends from Latin unus, one or a single one. Uses as a number, an indefinite article and a pronoun developed around that source; feminine une belongs to the same series.

université.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Medieval Latin universitas (specifically universitas magistrorum et scholarium 'guild/corporation of masters and students', from Classical Latin universitas 'the whole, aggregate, totality', derived from universus 'all together, whole').

urbanisme.etymology: Coined in the late 19th–early 20th century (attested in French around 1910, following Ildefons Cerdà's Spanish urbanización / urbanismo) from Latin urbanus ('of a city, urban', from urbs 'walled city') + suffix -isme.

urgence.etymology: Derived in the 18th century from urgent ('pressing, urgent', borrowed from Classical Latin urgens, present participle of urgere 'to press hard, push, drive, urge on') + suffix -ence.

user.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *usare ('to use frequently, make use of'), frequentative built on usus, past participle of Classical Latin uti ('to use, employ'); in French developed both the intransitive sense 'to make use of' (user de) and the transitive sense 'to wear out by use'.

history.meaning: to use (de); to wear down, wear out

utiliser.etymology: Utiliser was formed in French from utile ('useful', from Latin utilis, itself from uti 'to use') + verbal suffix -iser.

valise.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian valigia ('travelling bag, saddlebag'), a word of debated origin (often linked to Medieval Latin valisia). It replaced older words for leather saddlebags and became the standard French word for a suitcase.
valise.notes: Faire sa valise = to pack one's suitcase; boucler sa valise = to zip/fasten one's bag.

valoir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin valere ('to be strong, be vigorous, be worth, have value or influence'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- ('to be strong, rule').

valse.etymology: Borrowed at the end of the eighteenth century from German Walzer ('waltz', literally 'revolving dance'), agent noun from walzen ('to roll, revolve, glide in circles').

cognates.meaning: dance in 3/4 time (also borrowed from German Walzer)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: valse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: valse

vanne.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin venna ('wicker fish-weir or sluice barrier in a river', attested in 6th–8th century Frankish texts), of Gaulish origin (*venna 'wicker enclosure, weir').

vapeur.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin vapor, vaporem ('steam, warm exhalation, mist').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vapeur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vapeur

vapeur.notes: Like other Latin *-or* abstract nouns (**la chaleur**, **la couleur**, **la douleur**), **la vapeur** became feminine in French, though **un vapeur** (m) meant a steamship!

vase.etymology: Two homonyms of distinct origin: (1) masculine vase ('vessel, vase'), borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin vas, vasum ('vessel, container'); (2) feminine vase ('silt, mud'), borrowed in the 14th century from Middle Dutch wase ('mud, mire', from Proto-Germanic *wasōn).

velours.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Old Occitan velos ('shaggy, velvety cloth', altered in northern French to velours by suffix substitution), inherited from Classical Latin villosus ('shaggy, covered with soft nap'), from villus ('tuft of soft hair, nap').

cognates.meaning: velour borrowed from French velours; velvet via Anglo-Norman veluet

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: velours (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: velours

velours.notes: Remember that the final *-s* in **le velours** **/vəluʁ/** is silent, and **faire patte de velours** means 'to draw in one's claws and act with gentle charm'.

vendeur.etymology: Derived in the 12th century (Old French vendeor) from vendre ('to sell', from Classical Latin vendere) + the agent suffix -eur (from Latin -atorem / -itorem).

vendre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vendere ('to sell, offer for sale'), contraction of older venum dare ('to put up for sale'), from venum ('sale', accusative of *venus, from PIE *wesno- 'price, sale') + dare ('to give, put').

history.meaning: to offer for sale -> to sell

vendredi.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin Veneris dies / Vulgar Latin *Veneris diem ('day of Venus', goddess of love, translating Ancient Greek hēmera Aphroditēs).

venir.etymology: Venir descends from Latin venire, with the same basic meaning to come. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Its many later constructions still use the idea of something arriving or coming about, including its use as a helper in venir de followed by an infinitive.

vent.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin ventus (accusative ventum 'wind, breeze, air'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁ntos ('blowing, wind', participial derivative of *h₂weh₁- 'to blow').

vente.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vendita ('sale'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin vendere ('to sell', replacing Classical past participle venditus).

ventilateur.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from English ventilator (coined in 1743 by Stephen Hales from Classical Latin ventilator 'winnower', agent noun from ventilare 'to toss in the air, fan, winnow', from ventulus, diminutive of ventus 'wind').

vernis.etymology: Inherited from Old French verniz / vernis ('golden resinous finish'), via Medieval Latin vernix / veronix from Medieval Greek beroníkē, named after the Cyrenaican city of Berenice (modern Benghazi), famed in antiquity for exporting fragrant sandarac resin.

history.meaning: city of Berenice -> golden resin exported from there

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French vernis / vernisser

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vernis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vernis

vernis.notes: In the 19th century, painters brushing a final coat of **vernis** onto canvases on the eve of an exhibition gave the world **le vernissage** ('opening-night art reception').

verre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vitrum ('glass; woad'), which evolved through Vulgar Latin *vedro -> Old French voirre -> verre.

vers.etymology: Two homonyms inherited from Latin: (1) preposition vers ('toward, around'), from Classical Latin versus ('turned in the direction of, toward', past participle of vertere 'to turn'); (2) noun vers ('line of poetry, verse'), from Classical Latin versus ('furrow, line of writing, verse', also from vertere).

history.meaning: to turn -> turned toward (prep.); furrow, line of verse (noun)

verser.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin versare ('to turn often, tilt, overturn, pour out'), frequentative of vertere ('to turn').

history.meaning: to turn -> to tilt, overturn, pour

vert.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *virdis, syncopated form of Classical Latin viridis ('green, fresh, vigorous, youthful'), derived from virere ('to be green, flourish').

veste.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century from Italian veste ('garment, robe, waistcoat'), itself inherited from Classical Latin vestis (accusative vestem 'garment, clothing').

victoire.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin victoria ('victory, conquest'), derived from victor ('conqueror, winner'), agent noun from vincere (past participle victus 'to conquer, overcome').

vide.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vocitus ('empty, unoccupied'), a participial derivative of *vocare (dialectal/archaic variant of Classical Latin vacare 'to be empty, be void, be free').

vider.etymology: Derived in the 11th–12th century (Old French vuidier) from the adjective vuit / vuide ('empty', modern vide, from Vulgar Latin *vocitus) or directly from Vulgar Latin *vocitare ('to make empty').

vie.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vita ('life, way of living, existence'), derived from the root of vivere ('to live', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós 'alive').

vieux.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *veclus, syncopated form of Classical Latin vetulus ('little old one, old, aged', diminutive of vetus 'old, ancient').

vif.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vivus (accusative vivum 'alive, living, lively, brisk'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós ('alive'), cognate with vivere ('to live').

history.meaning: alive (in set phrases), lively, keen, bright

ville.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin villa ('country house, rural estate, farmstead'), which in Carolingian and Gallo-Romance usage shifted from 'manorial estate' to 'village', and finally in Middle French to 'town, city' (displacing cité into the sense 'ancient/walled core').

vinaigre.etymology: Transparent Old French compound of vin ('wine', from Latin vinum) + aigre ('sour, sharp, tart', from Latin acrem), literally 'sour wine'.

cognates.meaning: borrowed directly from Old French vinaigre

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vinaigre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vinaigre

vinaigre.notes: Because its mild acetic acid dissolves limescale without leaving a film, **le vinaigre blanc** has been a traditional French window-cleaning secret for generations.

vingt.etymology: Vingt continues later Latin vinti, an altered form of viginti, twenty. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.

vingt-cinq.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from vingt ('twenty', from Classical Latin viginti) + cinq ('five', from Latin quinque / *cinque).

vingt-huit.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from vingt ('twenty', from Classical Latin viginti) + huit ('eight', from Classical Latin octo).

vingt-neuf.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from vingt ('twenty', from Classical Latin viginti) + neuf ('nine', from Classical Latin novem).

vingt-quatre.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from vingt ('twenty', from Classical Latin viginti) + quatre ('four', from Classical Latin quattuor).

violon.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian violone / violino (built on viola 'viol', sharing the medieval Provençal and Italian string-instrument family of Old Occitan viola).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: violon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: violon

violon.notes: Lyon and Mirecourt became major French centers of **la lutherie** from the 16th century onward, crafting **violons** right alongside Italian Cremona.

virage.etymology: Derived in the 17th–19th century (first in nautical usage 'turning a ship or capstan', then in cycling and road transport 'curve, bend in a road') from virer ('to turn, veer', from Vulgar Latin *virare, probably from *vibrare or Celtic/Greco-Latin gyrus) + suffix -age.

history.meaning: turning, bend in a road, corner

vis.etymology: Inherited from Old French vis / viz ('winding vine tendril; spiral staircase; screw'), from Classical Latin vitis ('grapevine, vine tendril'), because of the spiral shape of a vine's tendrils.

viser.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *visare ('to look at attentively, gaze at, aim at'), frequentative of Classical Latin videre, past participle visus ('to see').

history.meaning: to see -> to look closely at, aim at
to aim at, sight; to endorse/stamp a document

visite.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 16th century from visiter ('to go to see, inspect, visit'), borrowed from Classical Latin visitare ('to go to see often, visit'), frequentative of visere / videre ('to see').

history.meaning: to see -> to go to see, visit
visit, call, medical or official inspection

vite.etymology: Inherited from Old French viste ('quick, nimble, prompt; quickly'), of debated origin: either from Vulgar Latin *vistus ('seen, alert, ready', from videre 'to see') or adapted from Classical Latin vegetus ('lively, vigorous, brisk').

vitesse.etymology: Derived in the 12th century (Old French visteche, vistesse) from the Old French adjective viste ('quick, nimble, fast', modern vite) + the abstract noun suffix -esse (from Latin -itia).

vitre.etymology: Learned or semi-learned medieval borrowing from Classical Latin vitrum ('glass'), specialised in French to mean a flat windowpane while inherited verre (also from vitrum!) kept the general senses 'glass material' and 'drinking glass'—a classic French etymological doublet.

rootFamily.gloss: glass (popular doublet from the same Latin vitrum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vitre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vitre

vitré.etymology: Participial adjective formed in the 14th–15th century from vitrer ('to fit with glass panes'), derived from vitre ('windowpane, glass', borrowed from Classical Latin vitrum 'glass').

history.meaning: window glass -> glazed, fitted with glass panes

vivant.etymology: Present participle of vivre ('to live', from Classical Latin vivere), used as an adjective ('living, alive, lively') and as a noun ('living person; lifetime').

vivre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vivere ('to live, be alive, subsist, reside'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti ('lives').

vocal.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin vocalis ('uttering a voice, speaking, sounding, vocal'), derived from vox, stem voc- ('voice').

voici.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French (voi ci) of the imperative vois ('see!, look!', from voir, Classical Latin videre) + the proximal adverb ci ('here', from Old French ici, from Vulgar Latin *ecce hic 'behold here').

history.meaning: see here! -> here is, here are

voilà.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French (voi là) of the imperative vois ('see!, look!', from voir, Classical Latin videre) + the distal adverb là ('there', from Classical Latin illac 'that way, there').

history.meaning: see there! -> there is, behold, that's it

voir.etymology: Voir continues Latin videre, to see. The Académie records the French verb from the tenth century.

voisin.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vecinus, alteration of Classical Latin vicinus ('near, neighboring; a neighbor'), derived from vicus ('row of houses, street, quarter, village').

history.meaning: hamlet, street -> belonging to the same street, neighbor

voiture.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vectura ('conveyance, transport, carriage, fare'), derived from vehere, past participle vectus ('to carry, convey in a vehicle').

history.meaning: means of transport -> carriage, railway car, automobile

voix.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin vox, accusative vocem ('voice, sound, utterance, word, vote'), from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs ('voice').

volant.etymology: Present participle of voler ('to fly', from Classical Latin volare), used as an adjective ('flying, loose, movable') and substantivized as a noun ('shuttlecock, flounce, flywheel, steering wheel').

volet.etymology: Formed on voler ('to fly, swing lightly', from Latin volare) + -et. After naming light fluttering ribbons, cloth sorting trays, and hinged triptych panels, un volet came in the seventeenth century to mean a hinged wooden shutter swinging open and shut across a window.

history.meaning: light cloth; hinged panel of a triptych

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: volet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: volet

volontiers.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin voluntarie ('of one's own free will, willingly') blended with adverbial -s, derived from voluntarius ('willing, voluntary', from voluntas 'will, desire').

votre.etymology: Votre descends from Popular Latin *voster (Classical Latin vester, 'your', built on vos 'you' by analogy with noster 'our'). As s before t fell silent in French, voster became vostre, modern votre.
votre.notes: Singular **votre** (*votre chambre*), plural **vos** (*vos clés*); stressed pronoun **le vôtre** keeps the circumflex.

vouloir.etymology: Vouloir developed from reconstructed popular Latin *volere, a remodelling of Classical Latin velle, to want. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. The asterisk marks the reconstructed form: it should not be mistaken for an ordinary quoted spelling from a surviving text.

history.meaning: a remodelled infinitive meaning to want

vous.etymology: Vous continues Latin vos, the second-person plural pronoun. The Académie dates it to the tenth century. Modern French uses this plural form both for several addressees and, politely, for one person.
vous.notes:
- Verb agreement is always plural: *vous êtes*, even for one person.
- Participles and adjectives agree with the real referent: *Vous êtes content* (one man), *contente* (one woman).

vous-même.etymology: Compound intensive/reflexive pronoun formed from vous ('you', inherited from Classical Latin vos) + même ('self, same', Old French meïsme, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, superlative of -met + ipse 'self').

voyage.etymology: Inherited from Old French veiage / voiage ('journey, expedition, pilgrimage'), from Classical Latin viaticum ('provisions or money for a journey; a journey'), derived from via ('road, way').

voyager.etymology: Derived in the 14th–15th century from voyage ('journey, trip', from Classical Latin viaticum) + the first-conjugation verbal ending -er.

voyageur.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century from voyager ('to travel', from voyage) + the agent suffix -eur.

voûté.etymology: Participial adjective of voûter ('to arch, vault, bend over'), derived from Old French volte / voute ('arched roof, vault', modern voûte, from Vulgar Latin *volvita, feminine past participle of Classical Latin volvere 'to roll, turn, curve').

vrai.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *veraius / *veracus, derived from Classical Latin verax ('speaking the truth, truthful') and verus ('true, real, genuine').

vraiment.etymology: Vraiment is a French derivative of vrai, true. The Académie records it from the twelfth century; its uses include both truly and the conversational intensifier really.

vue.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viduta ('sight, vision'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin videre ('to see', replacing Classical past participle visus).

vérifier.etymology: Vérifier was borrowed from Medieval Latin verificare ('to make true, confirm to be true', from verus 'true' + facere 'to make').
vérifier.notes: Everyday French verb for 'to check' (*vérifier la cave*, *vérifier l'adresse*).

vérité.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned adaptation in the 10th–11th century (Old French veritet) from Classical Latin veritas (accusative veritatem 'truth, reality, truthfulness'), derived from verus ('true').

vôtre.etymology: Inherited (via the stressed Old French form vostre) from Vulgar Latin *voster, reshaped from Classical Latin vester ('your, yours', formed on vos 'you' by analogy with noster 'our').

week-end.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century (attested in French around 1906) from English week-end / weekend, compound of week (Old English wice) + end (Old English ende).

history.meaning: end of the week, Saturday–Sunday break

y.etymology: The pronoun y continues Latin hic, here. The Académie records it from the ninth century. It is a different dictionary entry from the name of the letter y.

zéro.etymology: Borrowed in 1485–1515 from Italian zero (contracted from zefiro), from Medieval Latin zephirum (introduced by Fibonacci in 1202), adapted from Arabic ṣifr ('empty, nothing, zero'), a calque of Sanskrit śūnya ('void, zero').

à.etymology: À principally continues Latin ad, towards or for. Later spoken Latin extended its grammatical uses into relationships now expressed with à in French. The Académie also identifies a separate source a(b) in some expressions, so not every use has one simple origin.

âge.etymology: Âge was formed with the suffix -age from older French aé or ée, continuing Latin aetas, age. The Académie records early forms e(d)age and aage.

âgé.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from âge ('age, time of life', Old French aage / eage, from Vulgar Latin *aetaticum, derived from Classical Latin aetas 'time of life, age') + participial adjective suffix -é.

history.meaning: of a specified age; elderly, aged

ça.etymology: In its everyday pronoun use, ça is a shortened or altered form of cela. The Académie dates that use to the seventeenth century. The psychoanalytic noun has a separate later history.

ébrécher.etymology: Formed in the 12th–13th century (Old French esbrechier) from prefix é- (Old French es-, from Latin ex- 'out') + brèche ('breach, gap, notch', borrowed from Frankish *breka 'breaking, gap', from *brekan 'to break').

history.meaning: to chip, notch the edge of a blade or vessel

écart.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 16th century from écarter ('to set apart, separate, move aside'), from Old French escart / esquarter ('to quarter, scatter, set apart'), from Vulgar Latin *exquartare (from ex- + quartus 'fourth').

échanger.etymology: Inherited from Old French eschangier ('to exchange, barter'), from Vulgar Latin *excambiare, compound of ex- ('out') + Late Latin cambiare ('to barter, exchange', of Gaulish origin *kambion).

échelle.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin scala ('ladder, flight of steps', related to scandere 'to climb'). Spoken Latin added a prosthetic vowel before initial sc- (*escala), yielding Old French eschiele, then échelle.

cognates.meaning: graduated measure; to climb (via Latin scala)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: échelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: échelle

écho.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin echo, from Ancient Greek ēchō ('reflected sound, personified nymph Echo'), related to ēchē ('sound, ringing noise').

éclabousser.etymology: Attested in the 16th century (esclabousser 'to spatter with mud or water'), an expressive blend of éclater ('to burst, fly into splinters') and regional/Old French esbousser ('to dirty with mud or dung', from bouse 'cow dung').

history.meaning: to burst/fly + spatter with mire -> to splash, spatter

éclair.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century (Old French esclair) from éclairer ('to flash lightning, light up'), from Vulgar Latin *exclariare ('to make bright, flash'), from ex- + clarus ('bright, clear').

history.meaning: flash of lightning; cream-filled pastry (since c. 1860)

éclairer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exclariare (alteration of Classical Latin exclarare 'to make bright, illuminate, clarify'), compound of ex- ('out, thoroughly') + clarus ('bright, clear').

école.etymology: Inherited (with prosthetic vowel before initial sc-) from Classical Latin schola ('leisure given to learning, lecture, school'), borrowed from Ancient Greek scholē ('leisure, spare time, philosophical discussion, school').

écouter.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ascultare (dissimilated from Classical Latin auscultare 'to listen attentively, overhear, obey').

écran.etymology: Inherited from Old French escran ('fire-screen, wicker or wooden shield against heat or wind'), borrowed from Middle Dutch scherm or Frankish *skrank / *skirm ('protective barrier, screen, shield').

history.meaning: fireplace heat shield -> projection or display screen

écrire.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin scribere ('to scratch, engrave, draw lines, write'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ- ('to scratch, incise').

écriture.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned adaptation in the 11th–12th century (Old French escriture) from Classical Latin scriptura ('writing, composition, scripture'), derived from scriptus, past participle of scribere ('to write').

énigme.etymology: Learned Renaissance borrowing from Classical Latin aenigma, itself from Ancient Greek aínigma ('riddle, dark saying'), derived from ainíssomai ('to speak in hints', from aînos 'meaningful tale').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: énigme (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: énigme

énigme.notes: Watch the gender: although Latin *aenigma* was neuter, **une énigme** settled in modern French as a feminine noun.

énormément.etymology: Formed in the 15th century from the adjective énorme ('outside the norm, immense, huge', borrowed from Classical Latin enormis, from ex- 'out of' + norma 'carpenter's square, rule') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

épais.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin spissus ('thick, dense, crowded, compact, slow').

épaule.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin spatula ('broad flat blade, shoulder-blade, shoulder of an animal'), diminutive of Classical Latin spatha ('broad flat wooden blade, paddle, broadsword', from Ancient Greek spathē).

history.meaning: broad blade -> small flat blade, shoulder-blade

épicerie.etymology: Derived in the 13th–14th century (Old French espicerie) from épice ('spice', inherited from Late Latin species 'wares, spices, drugs') or épicier ('spice merchant, grocer') + suffix -erie.

épicier.etymology: Derived in the 12th–13th century (Old French espicier 'apothecary, merchant of spices and drugs', or from Medieval Latin speciarius) from épice ('spice', inherited from Late Latin species 'goods, spices, kinds', Classical Latin 'appearance, sort').

history.meaning: kind, sort -> spices, drugs -> spice dealer

éponge.etymology: Inherited via Old French esponge from Latin spongia, borrowed from Ancient Greek spongía ('sea sponge'). Gallo-Romance added a vowel before initial sp- (*ispongia -> esponge -> éponge).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: éponge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: éponge

éponge.notes: Initial **é-** regularly corresponds to English *s-* before *p, t, c* (**éponge** / *sponge*, **étoile** / *stellar*, **école** / *school*).

époque.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Medieval/Modern Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek epochē ('cessation, fixed point in time from which years are reckoned, astronomical position'), derived from epechein ('to hold back, stop, pause').

history.meaning: to pause, check -> fixed reference point in time

équipe.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 15th century ('line of barges towed together, work gang') from équiper ('to fit out a ship, supply'), derived from Old French eschipre / esquif, from Old Norse skipa ('to man or fit out a ship', from skip 'ship').

history.meaning: ship -> to man/fit out a vessel
fitted boat crew, work gang -> team, crew

équitation.etymology: Équitation is a sixteenth-century borrowing from imperial Latin equitatio, horse riding. Its history is a specific Latin borrowing rather than a generic story inferred from the French ending.

étage.etymology: Étage comes from Old French estage ('dwelling, floor level', from Vulgar Latin *staticum, built on stare 'to stand' — a 'standing level'). English 'stage' was borrowed from Old French estage.
étage.notes: Remember French floor numbering: **le rez-de-chaussée** = ground floor, **le premier étage** = one flight up.

étagère.etymology: Eighteenth-century derivative of étage ('storey, tier, level', from Old French estage 'standing place, level', built on Latin stare 'to stand'): originally an open piece of furniture with stacked tiers of shelves, then any individual shelf.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étagère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étagère

état.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in the 12th–13th century (Old French estat) from Classical Latin status ('standing, posture, condition, rank, public order'), action noun from stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: state, condition, social estate, body politic

éteindre.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extingere (reshaped from Classical Latin exstinguere 'to quench, put out a fire, wipe out'), compound of ex- ('out') + stinguere ('to quench, prick out').

history.meaning: to quench, put out a flame
to extinguish, put out, switch off

étiquette.etymology: From Middle French estiquette ('small pointed peg or paper slip stuck onto a courtroom sack of legal files'), derived from Old French estiquier ('to stick, pierce'), borrowed from Frankish *stikkan ('to prick, stick fast').

history.meaning: identifying label pinned to a file bag; court protocol card

cognates.meaning: ticket and etiquette both come from French étiquette!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étiquette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étiquette

étiquette.notes: Written slips (**étiquettes**) listing ceremonial rules at royal courts gave Europe the word **etiquette**, while earlier Middle French **estiquet** gave English **ticket**.

étoile.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stēla (with long ē, altered from Classical Latin stella 'star'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr ('star').

étonnamment.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from the adjective étonnant ('astonishing, surprising', present participle of étonner) + the adverbial suffix -ment (with assimilation of -nt + -ment to -mment).

étonnant.etymology: Present participle used as an adjective (since the 16th century) of étonner ('to stun as if by thunder, astonish, surprise'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *extonare (Classical Latin attonare 'to strike with thunder, stun', from tonare 'to thunder').

history.meaning: to stun -> to astonish -> astonishing, surprising

étrange.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin extraneus ('external, foreign, from outside, strange'), derived from extra ('outside, beyond').

étranger.etymology: Derived in the 12th century (Old French estrangier) from Old French estrange ('foreign, from outside', modern étrange, from Classical Latin extraneus) + suffix -ier, taking over the sense 'foreign, foreigner, stranger' as étrange specialized to 'odd'.

étroit.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin strictus ('drawn tight, compressed, narrow, close'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, squeeze'; doublet of learned strict).

history.meaning: to bind tight -> drawn together, narrow

étui.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French estuier ('to enclose safely, treasure, keep with care'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *studiare ('to tend zealously to', from Classical Latin studium 'care, zeal').

history.meaning: to sheathe safely -> protective fitted case

cognates.meaning: learned cousin from the same Latin studium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étui (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étui

étui.notes: Unlike a boxy **boîte**, **un étui** follows the shape of the treasured object inside (**un étui à violon**, **un étui à lunettes**).

été.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin aestas, accusative aestatem ('summer, summer heat'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- ('to burn, glow'). (Homonymous past participle été 'been' comes from Vulgar Latin *essitus / Classical Latin status.)

éviter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin evitare ('to shun, avoid, escape from'), compound of ex- ('out of, away') + vitare ('to shun, avoid').

être.etymology: Être combines two historical sources. Its main line is Latin esse through reconstructed popular Latin *essere. Forms such as étant, été and étais also continue Old French estere, from Latin stare, meaning to stand or remain.

history.meaning: to stand or remain; from Latin stare

être.notes: Être is highly irregular. It forms compound tenses with reflexive verbs and with verbs such as aller, venir and partir. Many other verbs of movement use avoir, so learn the auxiliary with the verb.

œil.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin oculus (accusative oculum 'eye; bud of a plant'), diminutive formation from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- ('to see; eye'). Its irregular plural yeux continues the Latin accusative plural oculos.

œuf.etymology: Œuf comes from Popular Latin *ovum (Classical Latin ovum, 'egg'). Notice how French pronounces the final f in the singular **un œuf** (/œf/) while dropping it in the plural **des œufs** (/ø/), reflecting Old French sound changes before plural -s.
